Furthermore, we establish a connection between deformed Casimir operators and the Casimir operator of the underlying Lie algebra. We also discuss how deformed quantum mechanical systems can be interpreted through matrix models. We reject the common idea that deformed Casimir operators fail to commute with each other. In this study, a high-speed optical transmission system is demonstrated, achieving a data rate of 72Gbit/s using the on-off keying technique, over a distance of 18.8km in a South China Sea submarine cable that lacks dispersion compensation.  Chromatic dispersion in this underwater cable causes four signal nulls in a 36GHz bandwidth, severely hindering BER performance. To address this issue, a decision feedback equalizer was initially applied with satisfactory results, however its effectiveness was impeded due to the occurrence of burst errors resulting from unpredictable marine conditions. To mitigate this issue, a weighted DFE method was developed but proved insufficient as it was unable to fully compensate for the spectral distortions due to the limited scope of its feedback symbols. To address this limitation, the introduction of maximum likelihood sequence estimation after WDFE proved capable of both rectifying the spectral distortions and providing optimal detection, ultimately yielding a maximum 2.9dB enhancement in signal quality and eliminating BER floors, thereby providing a viable solution for mitigating the detrimental effects of burst-error propagation in fiber-optic communications systems. This approach was successfully validated through actual underwater field trials. Additionally, a weighted feedforward equalizer was explored as a potential means of resolving this issue, however this approach was discarded in favor of the WDFE method due to its superior performance. Furthermore, a discussion on the advantages anddisadvantages of various FF and FE methods was conducted, providing insight into their applicability in underwater fiber communications systems. Ultimately, this research provides a groundbreaking breakthrough in resolving the spectral distortion-induced BER degradation in such systems. To facilitate further research and system design, a 3D graphical representation of various FF and FE methods, including WDFE and MMSE-FFFE, was included as an appendix to this document. With this breakthrough, high-speed underwater fiber communications systems are now capable of achieving error-free data transmission over a distance of 18.8km, even in the presence of burst errors resulting from unpredictable marine conditions. Consequently, this research is a significant contribution to the field of underwater fiber communications, enabling the development of reliable and efficient communications systems for underwater applications. Furthermore, this breakthrough has the potential to accelerate the deployment of underwater fiber communications systems, particularly those requiring high data rates, thereby opening up new possibilities for underwater communication and collaboration. Deep Learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs utilize a convolution-based approach to facilitate efficient and flexible information extraction across varying time spans. Nonetheless, TCNs face a significant challenge in accurately capturing remote temporal dependencies, a problem that limits their practical application. We introduce a Pre-processing technique called Pruning In Time (PIT), which employs a careful filtering method to select relevant historical data points for each timestamp. By leveraging this strategy in conjunction with common optimizers such as PIT-L1 and PIT-L2, we have found that it significantly enhances the model's performance on benchmark datasets including the ETS dataset. Furthermore, our models exhibit superior performance when compared to state-of-the-art methods in multiple tasks including event detection, classification, and prediction. The source code of our method has been made publicly available on GitHub. On further investigation, we discovered that PIT enables better performance than both sparse attention and general purpose pruning methods. Moreover, our results indicate that PIT has a minimal impact on model size, achieving a max of 1.2x at a 30% pruning rate, in contrast to 5x for uniform pruning. The reason for this is due to the careful filtering method employed by PIT, which only removes a limited number of filter weights from the model. As a result, our models exhibit a max of 1.5x increase in inference time when compared to their non-pruned counterparts, in contrast to 2x for uniform pruning. Overall, our results demonstrate the effectiveness of PIT in improving the performance of TCNs on time-series data, a benefit that accrues with both event prediction and prediction tasks. The fact that PIT is a simple yet highly effective method suggests that other DL models that rely on temporal data may also derive a significant benefit from this optimizer. The fact that the models optimized with PIT by the authors achieved state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmark datasets including the ETS dataset, the Activity Recognition dataset, the Cosmic Ray dataset, the Electric Load dataset, the Weather dataset, and the Motorima dataset, among others, further underscores the wide-ranging benefit of this optimizer. While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth has been challenging. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory and a similar telescope at the Cherenkov Telescope Array site to improve the precision of this technique to a precision of possibly 0.01. To accomplish this, we conducted precise laboratory measurements of the system's response to varying light intensities and spectra to counter the limitations of non-linear CCD detectors under observation conditions. We utilized a novel statistical approach to handle the calibration uncertainty and the noise of the CCDs, and tested our method using data from the FRAM telescope exposed to two different types of aerosols: the clean Atlantic atmosphere and the dusty atmosphere over the Chaco National Park in Paraguay. Our technique accurately captured the expected increase in aerosol depth at the latter location. Furthermore, our team investigated the sensitivity of this technique, discovering that it can distinguish between tiny variations in the optical depth, especially in environments with low aerosol levels, and that it can also detect variations in the angular scattering phase of aerosols, such as polychromatic observations with a relatively low cost implication of extending our technique to the CTA cameras. In order to achieve the best results with this technique, we recommend using a specific exposure time and adjusting the camera's gain based on the ambient temperature, humidity, and detection system characteristics. Additionally, our team explored potential systematic errors related to this technique, including uncertainties associated with the calibration of the system, atmospheric conditions, and variations in the detection system over time, and established a plan to further investigate some of these uncertainties in the future. Nonetheless, our technique has already led to an early detection of a well-known dust storm over the Atlantic Ocean several hours before it was identified by satellite, and it continues to contribute valuable data to the development of the CTA. In light of these advancements, we believe that this technique has the potential to become a leading method for monitoring aerosols in the sky, particularly when combined with the unprecedented sensitivity and coverage provided by the next-generation CTA cameras. Ultimately, by accurately determining the aerosol depth over a broad altitude range, this technique may also provide a valuable means of calibrating the system's response to varying light intensities

Recently, deep learning methods have achieved high accuracy in pose estimation;  however, estimating a pose using only one image, known as single-image estimation, remains a challenge.  To overcome this, researchers typically use multiple images at once, but this can be more complicated than estimated poses are likely to be.  One approach that has shown promise in recent years is clustering-based single-image estimation, where the goal is to group features from one image into sets of four to determine a pose.  We have taken this approach a step further by creating a model that uses both clustering and correspondence learning to estimate a pose from one image.  Our model uses a deep learning method that combines two types of clustering strategies, projected clustering and correspondence learning, to analyze the features from one image.  This approach allows our model to estimate a pose with high accuracy, especially on datasets with a wide range of scales and occlusions.  We have tested our model against the leading deep learning pose estimation models and found that it performs at least as well as, if not better than, these models on every dataset we used.  We have also included a video with our results to show how well our model works in practice.  One key factor that contributed to the success of our approach was our decision to use two types of clustering strategies.  We had considered using just one strategy, but we were unsure which one would work best.  To make this decision, we created a simple test using a single image of a person whose pose we already knew.  We then used this image to train our model and saw how well it performed compared to the actual pose.  We ran this test for both projected clustering and correspondence learning to make sure that our choice was the best one.  Our test showed that using correspondence learning resulted in more accurate estimates than using projected clustering.  We found that using correspondence learning led to more accurate estimates because it produced a more compact group of features than projected clustering.  We then used this knowledge to guide our implementation of the correspondence learning module in our model.  We hope that our test will be helpful to other researchers who are considering using clustering strategies to estimate a pose from one image.  One potential extension to our model involved using a different type of correspondence learning module that uses a neural network to analyze the features from one image. Traditionally, the Metropolis-Alberto algorithm has been the standard method for this purpose; however, it poses issues with energy conservation and fluctuation control, particularly in complex electronic systems undergoing slow structural changes. This limitation can result in the introduction of an artificial barrier in energy landscapes, hindering the algorithm's efficiency in sampling configurational aspects. To address this challenge, we developed a Monte Carlo method based on the Langervin Dynamics algorithm, which leverages the benefits of numerical integration while avoiding the need for explicit time steps. By introducing an implicit step size for momentum updates, we created a method that seamlessly integrates the interaction between system momentum and potential energy, allowing for more precise fluctuation control and higher acceptance rates in metastable regions, thus significantly enhancing the efficiency of Monte Carlo simulations. When compared to the Metropolis-Alberto algorithm, our proposed method yields substantial gains in computational cost, with cases showing improvements of up to ten million-fold in energy evaluations per second. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness through the simulation of gas-phase hydrogen chains, hydrogen molecules in magnetic fields, and the carbon dioxide molecule. Notably, our results also show that the proposed method successfully eliminates the artificial barrier issue with an energy gap in molecular nitrogen. Additionally, we anticipate it will have a significant impact on the development of hybrid molecular dynamics-Monte Carlo simulations, particularly in the integration of high-level electronic structure methods. Our proposed method will enable the seamless combination of numerical integration and Monte Carlo approaches, potentially revolutionizing the field of chemical physics. The Causal Exploration Toolbox is an open source Python framework that offers a diverse range of methods for actively discovering causal relationships directly from observations. As domain independence is a key feature, the toolkit is suitable for use in various settings, including individual learning scenarios, multi-agent environments with shared goals, and situations where the agent is rewarded internally. The framework is built on top of PyTorch and is designed for easy integration with popular reinforcement learning algorithms, allowing the agent to improve its performance by dynamic policy updates. A concise API is provided for convenient programing and tracking of the agent's state. Through the introduction of the Causal Exploration Toolbox, we aim to accelerate research in causal reinforcement learning by providing a standardized framework and a range of learning scenarios that help evaluate the performance of causal algorithms. This is especially important as the field's growth rate significantly outpaces the advancement in theoretical understanding, leading to a diverse range of methods that, despite their intuitive names, often lack clear definitions or comparisons. To further this research, we introduce three novel benchmark problems that focus on testing the ability of causal reinforcement learning algorithms to detect causal links, as well as integrate the toolkit with the Gym framework to facilitate easy implementation and reproduction of related work. Through extensive experiments using both traditional reinforcement learning agents and those equipped with causal models, we demonstrate the advantages of causal detection methods on a range of complex tasks. Additionally, our results show that the choice of intervention policy has a significant impact on the performance of causal reinforcement learning algorithms, highlighting a key research direction in the field. Lastly, we explore the interplay between causal reinforcement learning and natural exploration-exploitation tradeoffs, showing that careful selection of the intervention policy can greatly impact performance, and raising important questions about the conditions under which causal reinforcement learning provides a significant advantage over non-causal methods. As a leading area in reinforcement learning research, significant results involving causal networks are likely to have broad implications across the field. This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. In fact, at mid-range speeds, pinch-off times relate differently to fluid dynamics than they do at either low or high speeds, indicating that increased pressure within the forming splash dome plays a significant role. In addition, our findings include the shift from the deeper water-entrapment phenomenon to the surface-seal regime, and observations on the partial-seal, rippling-splash-dome patterns. These findings provide a foundation for further understanding of complex water-entry situations, such as those involving spheres moving diagonally or horizontally through water.

We investigated the challenges of robust reinforcement learning in scenarios where an adaptive adversary intentionally distributes corrupted rewards across episodes. The adversary has access to the agent's policy and learning dynamics, allowing it to strategically manipulate the rewards within each episode in response to the agent's actions. The agent's goal is to develop a learning algorithm that enables effective discovery of a corruption-free optimal policy despite the adversary's interference. The analysis of the sample complexity required for this achievement to occur yields a square-root dependence on the number of actions and a logarithmic dependence on the safety constraint parameter, indicating that the worst-case scenario presents a significant challenge for the agent. Furthermore, the conditions under which the agent can learn a robustly optimal policy are defined by boundaries that separate regions of high and low corruption levels, providing valuable insights for the design of robust reinforcement learning algorithms. The findings of this study are validated by a variety of simulations conducted across multiple scenario types. The development of the robustly optimal policy is learned through a bi-directional gradient descent algorithm, and the results of the study demonstrate the advantages of this algorithm over several alternative approaches. The code for the study is openly accessible on GitHub. The study explores extensions to more complex state-based corruption models, defined by graphs, and establishes lower bounds for the sample complexity required for the discovery of a corruption-free optimal policy in such environments, outperforming the performance of policy gradient methods under certain conditions. The study investigates the implications of corruption models with multiple states for the design of robust reinforcement learning algorithms and establishes a specific condition under which a bi-directional algorithm achieves the optimal sample complexity required for the discovery of a corruption-free optimal policy. The study is a significant contribution to the study of robust reinforcement learning algorithms due to its rigorous analysis of the problem, the clear definition of a relevant metric (the sample complexity required for the discovery of a corruption-free optimal policy), and its use of a clear definition of a corruption model. The study is a important milestone in the study of robust reinforcement learning algorithms because it addresses a problem of critical importance to the development of safe and reliable autonomous agents, establishes a set of rigorous conditions for the discoverability of a corruption-free optimal policy, and provides a comprehensive analysis of the conditions under which a bi-directional algorithm achieves the optimal sample complexity required for the discovery of a corruption-free optimal policy. We find that cubanite exhibits unique, spin-dependent orbital selection rules in its 1s core levels, specifically in X-ray absorption near-edge structure and extended X-ray absorption fine structure. A burgeoning field in quantum physics, known as multi-phonon physics, is driving research and development for both fundamental understanding and applications in metrology and communication systems. Quantum acoustic resonators serve as the ideal testing ground for multi-phonon phenomena through a combination of theoretical and experimental studies. The specific system studied consists of a semiconductor quantum dot driven by a laser, coupled to an acoustic cavity, and has exhibited remarkable multi-phonon properties, albeit previously described with a simplistic two-level quantum dot model. However, by accounting for both bright and dark excitons within the quantum dot model, the complexity of this system can be better represented. The inclusion of dark excitons particularly offers a pathway for overcoming a significant constraint in quantum acoustic systems, namely the requirement for a strong external magnetic field to achieve non-equilibrium condition. The added feature of a quasi-degenerate three-level system allows for massive anti-linear operations without dependence on magnetic field strength. The resulting performance improvement, facilitated by a strong interaction between the quantum dot and acoustic cavity, enables a substantial increase in multi-phonon transitions through a process known as the dark highway. Notably, this phenomenon can occur even when the laser is orthogonal to the acoustic cavity's polarization, allowing for a greater selection of suitable transitions. The increased flexibility in system design creates opportunities for reducing the necessary intensity of a driving laser by a factor of up to 100,000, a improvement especially valuable in the development of quantum acoustic systems. The enhanced performance of these systems may lead to the creation of a new class of coherent sound waves with much lower generation thresholds, enabling the exploration of a previously inaccessible regime in research. The improved performance of quantum acoustic systems may also facilitate the development of novel applications such as quantum acoustic metasurfaces and the ensembles of quantum acoustic resonators. Our investigation focuses on a 2D electronic lattice derived from a non-symmorphic wallpaper group, specifically the AII symmetry within the 2D wallpaper system. We are examining a herringbone lattice modulated in both spatial proximity and velocity, thereby incorporating both nearby interaction and next-nearest interaction in a non-symmorphic context. Our study reveals a pair of Dirac cones in this system, where the non-symmorphic operation results in a separation of the Dirac cones into two distinct sublattices. We demonstrate that this separation is achievable only in non-symmorphic systems through a combination of on-site and nearest-neighbor site-orbiting magnetic interactions. The achieved precision enables the adjustment of the Dirac cones' shape, where a small alteration in the spatial proximity leads to a transition from a Dirac cone to a capsular conduction band. Additionally, we find that the direction of the electron's spin orbiting multi-layers stacks can be modified to an extent where the spin-orbiting layers become opposing, thus providing an alternative method for adjusting the Dirac cones. A potential experimental verification of this model is proposed, utilizing a recent realization of a herringbone lattice made from graphene. Our calculations also indicate the possibility of enhancing the charge carrier velocity around the Fermi point by adjusting the velocity proximity parameter, potentially leading to faster control of the electron spin. A comparison with an equivalent commensal lattice reveals that the non-symmorphic lattice maintains stability inside the magnetic phase only if the on-site interaction is negative, whereas a small positive on-site interaction causes the system to become unstable in both non-symmorphic and commensal lattices. Nonetheless, both the non-symmorphic and commensal lattices exhibit robust against on-site instability in the case of nearest-neighbor interaction. Ultimately, our investigation highlights that the unique characteristics of non-symmorphic systems can give rise to exceptional electronic properties. Moreover, the intricate relationships between symmetry, interaction, and electron behavior pose significant challenges for the design of materials with desired electronic properties, thereby emphasizing the importance of a high degree of precision in material synthesis. This study presents a optimization approach known as Direct Transcription for Dynamic Enhancement. In regular process optimization, solutions are found using mathematical models that capture plant behavior. However, these models often lack the detailed dynamics present in process control systems. As a result, the models may not accurately reflect the system's performance under varying conditions, specifically when the model is used to model multi-agent systems in dynamic environments. To address this limitation, the study employs a technique called Direct Transcription for Dynamic Enhancement, which utilizes direct transcription to enhance the accuracy of process models by incorporating the system's dynamics. This approach was successfully applied to a critical case involving the simultaneous ventilation of two COVID-19 patients in separate rooms with different infection rates. The outcome showed significant improvement, achieving a reduction in the error by nearly an order of magnitude. The research highlights the potential benefits of this approach to tackle complex dynamic systems in process control systems. Additionally, the study underlines the significance of considering the dynamics of process control systems in optimal control problems to prevent performance degradation at startup or during significant changes in setpoints. The name of the proposed algorithm, Direct Transcription for Dynamic Enhancement, reflects its purpose. The study presents the algorithm through an illustrative case rather than a formal definition, as the problem domain is shared by the authors. Furthermore, the research is an outcome of the Biannual Process Control and Systems Engineering Workshop, aiming to disseminate innovative process control concepts to industry professionals. The study is an expression of gratitude to the workshop's contributors, particularly Dr. Serafin Haamit, Dr. Jiri Havlik, Dr. Srinivas Rao, and Dr. Ravi Kumar. The study is an attempt to share the algorithm's development with the broader process control community, leading to the decision to present it at the 2022 International Conference on Process Control (PC 2022) in Bratislava, Slovakia. The decision was further influenced by the opportunity to collaborate with Dr. Jiri Havlik and Dr. Serafin Haamit on submitting the study to the conference. Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed a innovative, self-contained CT-based algorithm called the Dilated Dense Focus Attention Unet (DDAUnet). By carefully selecting key layers from existing segmentation models, we created a reduced DDAUnet framework that consistently produced reliable results. Our algorithm was evaluated using a large dataset of CT scans containing lesions in the esophagus, and the results showed significant improvement over baseline models. Furthermore, our study demonstrated the feasibility of accurately identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus directly from CT scans with good precision. The code for this study has been made available open-source on GitHub. Moreover, DDAUnet performed well in a challenge hosted by the Medical Image Analysis Conference, ranking fourth among five teams. The excellent performance of our method suggests its potential for use in clinical settings for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus from CT scans. Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing and a core extraction technique, extensively used to retrieve text-based information for further analysis. One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on recognizing entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies apply linear models, which do not adequately capture the hierarchical nature of nested entities. This work overcomes this limitation by framing nested NER as a whole-part relationship among entities and proposing a new paradigm to incorporate all entity structures. Moreover, we introduce a novel graph-based XML structure that comprehensively represents all possible nested entity structures and devise a parsing algorithm to identify the corresponding XML tags from text. Our method is pre-trained through a combination of token-classification tasks, enabling robust entity structure parsing. Experimental evaluations on multiple datasets demonstrate our approach's superiority over linear models and other comprehensive structure parsing methods. Specifically, our method achieves an F-score of 79.11% on the standard ONNE2010 dataset, outperforming the best linear model by a significant 7.51% while improving the multi-instance strategy's F-score by 5.51%. Moreover, our method exhibits exceptional adaptability, achieving an impressive 82.50% F-score on the challenging ONNE2010 dataset when trained on a related dataset. Our method's versatility also enables the identification of complex entity structures, such as hierarchies and lists, with an F-score of 80.01% on the R18 dataset. Overall, our approach serves as a pioneering comprehensive structure parsing method for NER, establishing a new framework for future NER research. Additionally, we publicly release six challenging multi-instance datasets derived from existing NER datasets, along with their corresponding XML structures, to promote future NER advancements. These datasets focus on comprehensive structure parsing and include nested, hierarchical, and list structures, with our proposed method achieving an F-score of at least 10% higher than other methods on five out of six datasets. Our study's comprehensive structure parsing approach excels by accurately identifying complex entity structures and integrating information from multiple instances, demonstrating substantial potential for further exploration and development. Furthermore, our work's comprehensive structure parsing framework identifies potential issues with linear models, such as transformers, potentially limiting their effectiveness on certain NER tasks due to their restricted understanding of hierarchical relationships. We provide a novel computation of the number of bitangents to a plane quartic using tropical geometry. By showing that this computation is equivalent to counting the number of points in a specific tropical variety over the real numbers with signs, we make the broader claim that tropical geometry offers a feasible approach for addressing a common issue in algebraic geometry. Specifically, when determining the number of solutions to a system of equations defined by polynomials of the same degree, we can transform the problem into a more manageable 'point-counting' task by utilizing a specific type of geometric construction. As an additional consequence of this methodology, we prove the rationality of the number of bitangents to a plane quartic with singularities, a result that simplifies a previous proof by Lenard. Furthermore, our approach enables us to investigate the topology of the variety of bitangents to a singular plane quartic. Lastly, we discuss potential extensions of this methodology to a broader class of curves. By exploring these ideas, we are able to derive results on the number of bitangents to a plane quartic with specific types of singularities, such as double points with particular coordinates, as well as an interesting result on the number of bitangents to a plane quintic with a triple point. As a broader contribution, we are able to demonstrate that our geometry-based approach can solve problems on '$\mathbb{A}^1$-varieties' that involve counting points with signs over the real numbers, a result that has implications for our primary focus on bitangents to plane curves. Ultimately, our results on the number of bitangents to a plane quartic or a plane quintic with a triple point provide concrete examples in the field of algebraic geometry that can be analyzed using a combination of tropical and classical geometric methods. Code-mixing is a common communication approach used by multilingual individuals who switch between two or more languages within a single utterance. It enables clearer expression of thoughts and opinions, especially when a single language isn't sufficient to convey the intended message. Code-mixing poses significant challenges to NLP systems that can hinder their performance and reliability, particularly when they struggle to handle both languages used in an mixed input. In this article, we explore various code-mixing scenarios, studying patterns in scripts and assessing available datasets, datasets with both spoken and written language codes, and multimodal codes where written language is combined with sound. We also examine contextual factors such as cultural and societal influences on code-mixing and potential implications for NLP systems designed to operate across languages. We conclude by outlining potential research paths for NLP that can accommodate code-mixing and address related challenges, including improving system performance, enhancing usability and user trust, and making systems more versatile in handling different language codes. We believe that developing effective NLP systems capable of handling code-mixing will enable them to better serve multilingual communities and provide more accurate and reliable assistance. Our analysis of online activity and misinformation statistics reveals that the BGS is indeed observable in the data and is linked to changes in user behavior during the pandemic. Furthermore, we find that pre-vaccination COVID-19 surge-related misinformation dissemination peaked at a significantly higher altitude than the same timeframe in 2020, with analogous increases observed in vaccine-related misinformation. We also examined regional misinformation circulation patterns and discovered distinct seasonal variations in the eastern and western seaboards of the United States, with the former exhibiting more pronounced fluctuations. Euler-Arnold equations constitute a diverse group of sophisticated mathematical theories that find applications in various complex systems, characterized by minimal possible degrees of freedom, which include conformal field theories, geometric flows, superfluids, ferromagnets, and viscoelastic fluids. Notably, a common thread unites these disciplines - they are all governed by a specific subset of Euler-Arnold equations that can be derived from a unified approach using conformal field theory techniques. This connection enables researchers to leverage the expertise of both mathematical physics and applied mathematics communities to explore novel solutions to these equations and, conversely, utilize the solutions to these equations to gain insights into the behavior of these complex systems. Building on this foundation, this paper focuses on an essential yet non-trivial subclass of these equations that encompasses the universality classes of planar conformal field theories, for which both exact solutions and asymptotic approximations are available. By presenting the applicable conformal field theory methods, this study aims to provide an intimate glimpse into the intricate underlying mathematics that govern these highly nonlinear equations. As such, this work is primarily directed toward an audience of mathematicians and physicists who are familiar with the underlying concepts but may require a refresher on the applied methods. In contrast, readers who are primarily interested in applied aspects or novel solutions may find this background focus too detailed. In recognition of this insight, the primary author has incorporated the feedback from multiple reviewers to streamline the presentation and address the key criticisms raised in the review process. In response to the suggestions made by the reviewers, the revised version includes a clearer introduction, a more concise presentation, and a revised layout that better flows throughout the text. This study investigates the application of a monolingual lexicon knowledge base to Neural Machine Translation. When NMT models translate phrases, they often rely heavily on similar patterns seen during training, relying on general language skills rather than specialized translation knowledge. To improve this, we propose incorporating a monolingual knowledge base into the NMT model. This way, the model can draw upon its knowledge of the target language's word associations and part-of-speech patterns to inform its translation decisions. We test this approach using a particularly large English knowledge base and find that it leads to substantial improvements in translation quality, especially for difficult phrases. Our approach and data are also made available for further research. As NMT systems are increasingly used in high-stakes applications, exploring ways to effectively integrate knowledge and ontologies is vital to achieving the highest levels of accuracy and reliability. We argue that neural machine translation models can learn and make use of extensive knowledge bases, providing a pathway for future systems to build upon this knowledge and further refine their translations. This could enable these systems to generalize better when translating rare or idiomatic phrases, producing more consistent output when translating the same phrase multiple times, and facilitating improvements to the systems as a whole with each new piece of knowledge added. This, in turn, may allow these systems to perform better against tasks like paraphrasing, summarization, and generating new variations of existing text. We also examine the role of auxiliary loss functions in training these models with integrated knowledge bases and find that simply adding the knowledge-aware loss function is sufficient to produce the notable improvements seen in our results. This suggests that these models are capable of effectively integrating the target language knowledge base during training. We further explore the possibility of applying this approach to other NMT models and find that it is applicable across a range of models, leading to similar improvements in translation quality. This includes the transformer-based models currently at the forefront of NMT research, indicating that the proposed approach is a versatile solution with wide applicability. We also investigate the possibility of applying this knowledge-aware NMT model to low-resource language pairs and find that it is particularly well-suited to such challenges. This is because the model is able to leverage the knowledge base to inform its translation decisions, even in the absence of sufficient parallel data to train a high-quality base model. We test this approach using a pair of very low-resource language pairs and find that it leads to substantial improvements in translation quality, increasing the BLEU score by over 10 points. While significant progress has been made in automated conversation tasks, generating coherent text phrases remains a challenge. To tackle this issue, researchers have developed stateful models that retain information from previous conversations, enabling them to produce more coherent text phrases. However, existing stateful models fail to account for the human factors involved in verbal communication and do not accurately reflect the underlying processes that occur during meetings. Furthermore, they lack the ability to learn from multiple participants simultaneously. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a novel data representation approach called the Drive-Based Motivation Model, which utilizes a recurrent neural network to analyze verbal communication between human participants. The model incorporates a dual representation, leveraging both continuous and categorical features to capture the underlying dynamics and implement a motivation function to predict the likelihood of a particular word being selected by a given speaker. By applying this model to real-world meeting data, we demonstrate a significant improvement in performance on state-of-the-art stateful models and verify the necessity of considering multiple agents in models through a systematic evaluation process. The resulting model also exhibits superior performance in offline experiments and achieves commercialization in a leading human-machine interface product. The foundation theorem in combinatorics enables the representation of any element within a Coxeter group through an ordered sequence of generators. However, this approach is only universally applicable when considering finite Coxeter groups. The current investigation aims to broaden the foundation theorem's scope to include infinite Coxeter groups of the B-type by demonstrating that any element within these groups can be expressed uniquely as a reduced product of generators, subject to a specific ordering criterion. Furthermore, this research introduces the concept of "foundational length" to characterize the number of generators required to express an element in a specific order. We have established a link between foundational length and the grading system in a specific order, and we have also identified a universal sequence of generators that minimizes foundational length across all possible orderings. The term "standard" is used to describe the foundational length of elements within the highest rank of a Coxeter group's lattice structure. Notably, our findings indicate that standard foundational length equals the longest descending chain length in a Coxeter group of type B. The principles established in this research will facilitate a broader exploration of foundational lengths in Coxeter groups. The current investigation focuses on Coxeter groups of type B, and an open problem is to examine whether similar results can be applied to Coxeter groups of type D. The concepts introduced in this research are a combination of multiple fields, including Coxeter groups, combinatorics, and lattice theory. Our study proposes a theoretical framework that can quantify the uncertainty of functional parameters used in a function, integrating insights from both the variance-gamma model and the bootstrap method. This framework is particularly relevant to PDF fitting, where the functional parameter in question is the PDF itself. When fitting PDFs, it's common to minimize the difference between observed data and calculated results through functional parameters such as mean, scale, and shape. However, the choice of PDF is ultimately driven by the underlying physical processes that generate the distribution. As a result, certain properties of the PDF, such as moments, can be used to connect the physical world to the data, even if some properties may be inconsistent with the actual data, thus indicating a need to include uncertainties in the analysis. Our proposed framework can handle this kind of problem and reduces complex calculations to straightforward operations by leveraging the properties of functional parameters, variance, and gamma distribution. We show that the uncertainty of the PDF in question can be determined using mock data generated from a root mean squared deviation of 0.1, and demonstrate the utility of this framework for determining uncertainty on real data from Higgs boson peak fitting. Additionally, we examine the degree to which the interpretation of experimental results depends on the choice of PDF, an issue commonly ignored in physics experiments, and highlight the need for a systematic approach to selecting the most accurate results. Our study also raises important questions about the nature of statistics and the complexity of data fitting, and we anticipate that our proposed framework will contribute significantly to advancing the art and science of physics experiments. The team led by S. Sato, S. Nakamura, and M. Takahashi investigated various aspects of this phenomenon by examining multiple spin configurations at and below the clustering transition temperature. The relative strength of the site and bond interactions was varied from equal to predominantly site-based, with an emphasis on two scenarios: when the site interaction is nearly double the bond interaction and when the site interaction is around 1.5 times the bond interaction. The influence of specific initial conditions on the resulting magnetization was also examined, with the observation that particular spin configurations can result in cluster sizes that either significantly increase or decrease over time, with a particular condition causing a notable shift towards smaller clusters. The study concluded by exploring potential applications of these findings to better understand clustering in more complex systems. As a result, various dark matter candidates that involve the Dark Sector are being studied, often referred to as "dark sectors." Within this category, "dark electromagnetism" stands out as a particularly simple scenario that consists of a single new vector boson. In this report, we examine the fundamental characteristics of dark photons and their inherent properties when produced at the LHC, as well as the challenges associated with identifying them through experimentally verifiable signatures. We analyze three dimensions of SDO/AIA data for massive stellar eruptions, specifically supernovae and giant eruptions from two sources: SN 2010jh and SN 2003fg, and ASASSN-15lh along with its possible companion SN 2015G. Using high-critical-density plasma, we identify forward-directed shocks in SN 2010jh's and ASASSN-15lh's spectra and map their evolution in the star's envelope for approximately 200 days, tracing the shock's interaction with the envelope as it accelerates and eventually reaches the star's surface. The shock's temperature and density are consistent with non-relativistic wave dynamics, while its velocity matches expectations from persistent mass losses. Upon breaking through the surface, the shock becomes a relativistic blastwave with enhanced density, and we estimate its energy to be roughly one percent of the star's energy output over 200 days. This analysis supports the idea that massive stellar eruptions produce forward-directed shocks that heat the envelope and generate powerful blastwaves. If detected early enough, these shocks could serve as indicators for detecting extragalactic supernovae, particularly when combined with radio and X-ray observations. Furthermore, we find that SN 2003fg and SN 2015G exhibited similar shock dynamics, and ASASSN-15lh's massive shock may have contributed to its exceptionally bright appearance. We provide detailed analysis of multiple images, and all relevant data can be accessed through the ASASSN-15lh GitHub repository. Additionally, we explore theoretical aspects of these shocks, including how they may aid in detecting supernovae, and outline potential observations for future eruptions. $\tau$-tilting theory was first introduced nearly a decade ago by Adachi, Iyama, and Reiten and has since become a major area of study in the representation theory of finite-dimensional algebras. These notes have a dual purpose: to provide an approach for learning $\tau$-tilting theory through various examples and to mark the beginning of a larger project by compiling relevant material. Some essential $\tau$-tilting results are presented here along with proofs for several specific examples, building on a foundation of basic definitions and concepts. Furthermore, we explore connections between $\tau$-tilting theory and other important areas of representation theory, including local finitely generated algebras, tilting modules, and Serre's second conjecture. Additional topics, such as the representation theory of quivers, symmetric algebras, and Coxeter groups, are also touched upon. It is our hope that these notes will not only facilitate learning $\tau$-tilting theory but also inspire further research in the field. We conclude by presenting several open questions related to $\tau$-tilting theory. Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach is presented that employs vertex splitting to remove edge crossings, targeting a more feasible "no bogus loops" condition, which is defined as the absence of singly-connected subcircuits comprised of two edges. A specific algorithm is described for identifying and resolving instances of bogus loops in limited memory, and is proven to do so within O(1.83^n) time, and is capable of handling instances with millions of edges. Furthermore, this algorithm serves as a foundation for developing exact solutions using branch and bound, and is currently the most efficient general method for resolving the no bogus loops condition. Additionally, a heuristic approach is described that effectively identifies a large proportion of the smaller bogus loops, and is capable of handling very large instances at a significantly faster rate. This algorithm's performance is scrutinized through a variety of real-world testing scenarios, and is found to significantly improve the efficiency of layout animations. The code for this project is openly available on GitHub. The problem of incremental learning poses a difficulty, where a model is required to recognize new classes after being trained on new data. Another persistent issue in AI is dealing with unbalanced data, where certain classes have significantly more instances than others. Unbalanced data presents a challenge for the model, as it tends to focus on easily recognizable instances and neglects less prevalent classes. In real-world applications, AI systems often encounter situations where data classes are not only unbalanced but also shift over time, presenting an increasing number of new classes with more instances than others. This paper explores the question of whether current incremental learning methods are effective at handling unbalanced data and whether calibration techniques can enhance the performance on each class separately. To answer this, we conducted extensive experiments using several state-of-the-art incremental learning models and compared their performance to that of models trained on balanced data. Furthermore, we investigated the impact of different calibration techniques on the performance of each class. Our findings indicate that current incremental learning models perform inferior to their balanced data counterparts and fail to recognize less prevalent classes. Moreover, our results show that employing different calibration techniques yields better performance on certain classes, demonstrating the importance of selecting the technique based on the data distribution. Finally, we highlight potential avenues for future research in the realm of incremental learning and underscore the importance of developing methods that can adapt to data that shifts over time. Code is available at: https://github.com/JulianVargasCF/ICIL-Calibration-Comparison. Loosely based on this investigation, we propose a novel approach that integrates the use of different activation functions to enhance the detection of less prevalent classes. Our approach is designed to mitigate the difficulty associated with less prevalent classes by employing a neural quantization method for the detection of these classes in conjunction with a residual learning approach for the detection of more instances classes. Experimental results indicate that our proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art ICIL models on certain classes. Furthermore, our results show that our approach achieves better performance on less prevalent classes and yields a significant performance boost on new classes in the test set. Recent advancements in energy-efficient design have accelerated processor development, yet energy consumption continues to rise, necessitating innovative solutions. By leveraging asynchronous data transfer and utilization delays, our proposed HyperDegrade system shifts CPU frequencies from GHz to MHz ranges, achieving significant reductions in energy consumption without compromising performance. Through integration with existing cache hierarchies, HyperDegrade ensures safe and efficient operation, while also providing flexible configuration options to balance energy efficiency against potential increases in latency. Our evaluation of a range of applications and benchmarks reveals an average energy savings of nearly 70% without noticeable degradation in output, and a particular use case involving an image recognition AI model experiencing a 10% decrease in latency in favor of 80% less energy usage. The source code of our evaluation has been made publicly available. Through the deployment of HyperDegrade, we believe that energy-efficient CPUs can provide reliable computing foundations for critical infrastructure such as voting systems and medical devices. Furthermore, by enabling the support of longer CPU cycles, HyperDegrade paves the way for the utilization of less expensive binary translation techniques, reducing the computational burden and further promoting energy efficiency. Additionally, we explore the potential integration of HyperDegrade with existing multi-threaded applications and systems, and outline design considerations and potential paths forward for future research and development. Overall, our research demonstrates the feasibility and effectiveness of CPU frequency degradation, and we anticipate that this approach will be widely adopted across the industry. This paper examines the privacy concerns surrounding Vertical Federated Learning (VFL), a technique used for collaborative data analysis among multiple parties. We highlight the potential leaks in VFL, specifically focusing on label leakage, aggregation attacks, and real-world case studies. We also discuss novel techniques utilized in VFL, such as federated learning for classification with encrypted data and Inverse Transformation-based Inference Prevention. However, these techniques require significant communications between participants and do not address label leakage. Consequently, we introduce new strategies for label leakage prevention, including encrypted training and inference techniques, dimensionality reduction, and artificial data injection. We demonstrate the effectiveness of these strategies through comprehensive experiments and evaluate their implications for data privacy in VFL. Ultimately, we conclude that combining these strategies with encrypted learning techniques can provide robust privacy protection for participants in VFL. Additionally, we explore the interplay between the utilities derived from VFL and its privacy protections through various cryptographic methods. Finally, we discuss the potential applications and future directions for research in VFL, including the development of publicly available datasets and more sophisticated encryption methods. Kernel methods have proven highly effective in various machine learning applications, yet their scalability to large datasets is limited due to the computationally expensive nature of pairwise evaluations. Random Fourier Features were initially proposed to approximate kernel functions using randomized transformations, thereby enabling the use of kernel methods on larger data sets. While widely adopted, this method exhibits shortcomings, primarily stemming from its insensitivity to data characteristics. Consequently, we introduce a novel approach to kernel approximation, one that leverages data dependent Fourier features to enhance accuracy. Specifically, our approach involves employing localized random transformations to capture the unique patterns within a given dataset. We demonstrate and evaluate our method against state-of-the-art competitors, including random Fourier features and data dependent Fourier features based on entropy optimization. Our results show that our approach yields significant improvements in both accuracy and computational efficiency, outperforming random Fourier features by a factor of ten in terms of square error and achieving comparable performance to entropy based methods at a fraction of the computational cost. Furthermore, our method enables the development of a highly efficient linear SVM algorithm, one that surpasses the performance of its finite dimensional kernelized counterpart. This research paper examines conformally flat hypersurfaces of n-dimensional space (n is 4 or higher) within a hypersphere of n+2 dimensions. We start by classifying and describing these conformally flat hypersurfaces when they have constant M\"obius curvature under specific transformations. Next, we determine the conditions and characteristics for these hypersurfaces to exhibit non-trivial flexible M\"obius curvature properties. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates that when the M\"obius curvature of a hypersurface is zero, it corresponds to a flat conformally invariant property. Building on this understanding, the research focuses on identifying flexible M\"obius curvature characteristics on these conformally flat hypersurfaces. Specifically, we establish that when the M\"obius curvature of a hypersurface has a Laplacian eigenvalue, it implies that the M\"obius curvature itself must have a similar eigenvalue. This relationship between the M\"obius curvature and the Laplacian eigenvalue is a key aspect of the research. Moreover, we demonstrate that when the M\"obius curvature of a hypersurface is a linear combination of its Laplacian eigenvalues, it indicates that the M\"obius curvature itself must be a solution to the Laplace equation. This understanding allows us to conclude that a hypersurface with constant M\"obius curvature will necessarily have that same constant curvature. On the other hand, a hypersurface with non-constant M\"obius curvature will necessarily have conformally invariant flat properties at its points of flexible M\"obius curvature. This research provides a theoretical foundation for further study on the M\"obius curvature of conformally flat hypersurfaces. Using advanced medical imaging to guide surgical procedures requires high accuracy segmentation of critical anatomical structures. Though U-Net-based models have achieved remarkable results in segmenting adult hearts from CMR data, their performance in accurately identifying cardiac malformations present at birth poses a significant challenge. In this study, we investigate the potential of U-Net models to be transferred from adult data to treat children with rare CHDs, whose low incidence makes available data scarce. We examine the effects of cardiac deviation severity and available training sample sizes on model performance, finding that while U-Net models can learn from adult data and apply this to children, larger training sets significantly improve results. Interestingly, our data suggests that models trained on smaller datasets are better at handling more severe cardiac deviations. However, these findings could be refined by increasing the size and diversity of available training sets. We also compare the accuracy of these models to that of a cardiologist, finding some heart deviations are accurately identified by the models, but others are not. Given the limited data available, we examine the effects of data augmentation on training sets of up to 2000 samples, but this has little impact compared to the effects of varying the size of training sets alone. Finally, we explore the potential of these models to be applied in real-world clinical settings with positive results. In conclusion, U-Net models can be successfully transferred from adult data and used to accurately identify parts of the heart in children with rare CHDs, making them a promising tool for use in the clinical field. In order to integrate these models into their practice, cardiologists and surgeons need to understand how to use them correctly, especially in cases where the models' performance is less strong. We also recommend that the development of more high-quality training sets, along with ongoing research into how to use these models correctly in the clinical field, is necessary in order to integrate them properly. Additionally, more work is needed to understand how to optimize these models for the unique requirements of surgical procedures, as well as further research into other areas where medical imaging could be used to guide surgical procedures. Finally, we recommend that the development of more advanced models, such as attention U-Net, should be given consideration. We make several contributions to the field of medical imaging, specifically in the use of deep learning, the field of congenital heart disease, and the field of medical education. We also use a novel approach to determine the effectiveness of these models, by including a discussion on the statistical analysis, as well as several suggestions on potential areas for further research.

This concept is rigorously defined using a probabilistic approach based on the Wigner distribution function. The proposed strength of the Fermi gas distribution has been calculated and tabulated for various nuclei across the periodic table. Notably, there is a distinct threshold at approximately 72 (in units of 10^-3 MeV^-1) that distinguishes 'high-strength' Fermi gases from 'low-strength' ones. The former are characterized by strong pairing interactions and are consistent with superconducting properties observed in certain nuclei, whereas the latter are associated with astrophysical objects like neutron stars and white dwarfs, for which the pairing interactions are typically weak. The 'high-strength' regime is seen in subatomic systems like atomic nuclei, meson nuclei, and possibly in quark matter, suggesting a common thread in their distribution behavior. In contrast, the proposed strength distinguishes between the core and crust regions of a neutron star, with the latter exhibiting higher strength values due to different quark matter properties. The implications of this finding are that a wide range of distribution-based shell model applications, including nuclear reactions, pairing phenomena, and mechanical properties of finite nuclei, as well as the behavior of neutron stars and quark matter, can be refined by considering the proposed strength quantity. The general method of proportional testing has been established as a powerful tool for evaluating random number generators and other uniform distribution-based algorithms, and it has achieved notable success in testing the uniform distribution of multi-variate functions like hash functions and function mappings from R^n to R^m. However, its primary limitation is its incompatibility with algorithms that generate bimodal distributions, which include many commonly used random number generators, cryptographically secure hash functions, and maps from R^n to R^m. Our research aims to break down this limitation by introducing a framework for testing the uniform distribution of algorithms that generate bimodal distributions, which does so by leveraging the fundamental principles of proportional testing to produce a method compatible with a wide range of bimodal distributions specified by their probability density functions (PDFs). We then apply this framework to specific examples of bimodal distributions, including the distribution produced by the F2W random number generator, which was previously found to be inconsistent with a uniform distribution using traditional proportional testing. Our results demonstrate that the F2W distribution is actually equivalent to a bimodal uniform distribution, which our framework is able to verify as consistent with a uniform distribution for the first time. Furthermore, we anticipate this framework to contribute significantly to the evaluation of random number generators and other algorithms that generate bimodal distributions, which are ubiquitous in computing, cryptography, and simulation. Our experience with implementing this framework has also involved the development of a tool, which is now available for public use in conjunction with this publication. This tool has already been used to evaluate the randomness of multiple random number generators, which includes one generator that passed the test and another that failed it. Our research has also explored the concept of a proportionate test being performed on a combination of separate proportional tests, which has led to a key discovery. We have coined the term 'co-Uniform' to describe a distribution that maintains two distinct uniform components, which has allowed us to simplify our proof by assuming that a distribution adhering to the specified format for bimodal proportional testing will always be co-Uniform. Our research has provided multiple concrete examples of bimodal distributions, which can be reached through the combination of two proportional tests. We have further established that any distribution that can be combined from two separate proportional tests will always result in a distribution that can be identified as co-Uniform. Our experience with this research has involved the creation of an interactive proof of concept, which is now available for public review and can be found in the supplied code. Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which produces a face that varies based on the orientation and another face that remains invariant, then fuses these faces via a self-alignment mechanism informed by occlusion. Exhaustive testing of our proposed technique on the widely used AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets shows substantial performance enhancements over existing top-ranking methods. Furthermore, our method exhibits practical applications potential, as evidenced by its successful integration into a state-of-the-art 3D face reconstruction pipeline, resulting in a face reconstruction model called SOFRNet. This combined model achieves superior results on the Florence dataset, a notable achievement considering our primary focus was on developing a high-performing 3D face alignment system. A negative pressure room (NPR) in biolabs and infectious-control hospitals must meet stringent safety standards set by bio-safety levels (BSLs) to prevent potentially deadly pathogens from escaping into the surrounding environment. These facilities maintain negative air pressure relative to the outside space by using specialized systems to contain the microbes. Modern building management systems utilize differential pressure sensors (DPSs) to regulate and monitor NPR's air pressure. Our research reveals a non-intrusive vulnerability in these systems, where an attacker can induce resonance in DPSs using malicious audio at their natural frequencies, causing the sensors to malfunction. Our findings show that the resonant frequencies of most DPSs fall within the range of human hearing. We have demonstrated that we can design music capable of generating these resonant frequencies and, in doing so, trigger a significant discrepancy in pressure readings. Our research shows that the malfunctions induced by this technique can fool the building management systems, potentially allowing pathogens to escape from NPRs. Our study also demonstrates that the resonant frequency-based attack can target multiple rooms simultaneously. Furthermore, we were able to successfully test this technique at a fully functional FDA-approved NPR located within a biomedical facility. Our research offers several measures that could mitigate this type of attack. Our study also raises concerns about the security of other industrial control systems that utilize similar sensors and highlights the need for further research in this area. Our study is the first of its kind to examine the potential threats to NPRs and infectious-control hospitals and we hope it will spur further research in this field. We investigated the effectiveness of dynamic learning for large-scale image classification tasks. Dynamic learning allows a model to determine the optimal number of parameters to achieve the best balance between performance and efficiency. In our study, we applied this approach to large datasets, specifically ImageNet, and discovered that it yields superior results compared to traditional fixed-parameter models. In particular, we found that dynamic learning resulted in a 5% improvement in top-1 accuracy for small models (0.03% improvement for large models) and a 94% improvement in top-5 accuracy for small models (49% improvement for large models) in terms of memory usage. These gains came with a relatively small increase in computational cost (1% for small models and 5% for large models). Moreover, our analysis revealed that the performance benefits of large models arose from their ability to achieve higher accuracy on difficult images, whereas small models performed better on easier images. These findings provide insight into the advantages of dynamic learning and highlight its potential as a method to enhance model performance, aid in efficient model selection, and facilitate the interpretation of model size through the lens of learning dynamics. In light of these results, we propose the use of dynamic learning for a range of applications, including multi-task learning, few-shot learning, and robust learning against overfitting. In code, we report our results for various models, including EfficientNet, a leader in the ImageNet classification benchmarks, and make our learning dynamics data freely available for download. This data enables the creation of an interactive visualization tool, allowing users to explore dynamic learning data in detail. In addition, we introduce the concept of a learning curve matrix, a comprehensive representation of learning dynamics across all model sizes, and show how it can be used to identify optimal models in terms of performance and efficiency. This approach is useful not just for ImageNet but also for other large datasets and domains where such a matrix can be constructed. In such domains, we anticipate that dynamic learning will become a standard practice, revolutionizing the way models are developed and evaluated. In response to these findings, we suggest modifications to common evaluation metrics, such as top-1 and top-5 accuracy, learning rate, and batch size, to make them more reflective of the performance of models of different sizes. Furthermore, we believe that future research in deep learning should give due consideration to the insights gained from learning dynamics. In particular, we expect future breakthroughs to result from the integration of learning dynamics data with other forms of information, such as loss surface analysis and neural network architecture search

Namely, given a central tower for N contained within N^{}, we define a square for N based on the central tower's square for N^{}, and determine the index and depth of the resulting subfactor N phosphorylled with its central tower's square. It's proven that this process establishes a bijection between the set of central powers of a given subfactor's central tower and the set of its squares of a specific index and depth. Recent advances in neural network models, such as Hamiltonian Neural Networks (HNNs), have achieved remarkable results in learning both functional and differential properties. HNNs have been compared to baseline models in tasks like reconstructing training input data and testing functions. Our investigation extends beyond mere comparison, focusing on evaluating HNNs' ability to learn differential operators like derivatives. By analyzing HNN-based approximation of derivatives, we theoretically demonstrate that these networks can indeed learn derivatives. Additionally, our analysis provides insights into the optimal hyperparameter settings that minimize prediction error. To verify our findings, we conducted numerous experiments under different scenario conditions. Notably, our results show that when the input data is sufficiently sampled, HNNs can accurately learn both first and second-order derivatives with minimal error. Conversely, when data sampling is inadequate, the estimated derivatives are no longer precise. To mitigate this issue, we explored the incorporation of extra information in the form of auxiliary Hamiltonians. By integrating this additional data, we found that HNNs are capable of learning second-order derivatives even with limited sampling. Our research provides a theoretical framework for understanding how HNNs can learn differential properties and showcases the network's practical effectiveness in processing raw data across various conditions. Given the promising results obtained, we believe there are numerous applications waiting for the deployment of HNNs in contexts involving the analysis of raw data. Finally, we anticipate future research directions to focus on the HNNs' performance in (1) processing noisy data, (2) expanding the network's inverse problem-solving capabilities, and (3) combining the method with dimensionality reduction techniques. With these advancements, the HNN's potential use cases are sure to expand even further. To facilitate further investigation, we have made the HNN implementation publicly available. By sharing this work, we aim to contribute meaningfully to the ongoing development of neural network methods that can accurately capture and utilize raw data's inherent structure. Moreover, we hope this research will help identify promising candidates for solving real-world problems that involve analyzing raw data with inherent structure. Lastly, we wish to express our gratitude to all the researchers whose previous work has facilitated our discovery and enabled us to contribute significantly to the ongoing development of neural network methods. In recognition of their achievements, we have appended an extensive list of references at the paper's end. Additionally, we are more than happy to address any inquiries related to this research and eagerly look forward to engaging with the research community. The accompanying list contains a comprehensive range of citations. In conclusion, our investigation has provided invaluable insights

This consideration is crucial for creating robust AI systems that are capable of withstanding critical situations in areas like transportation, finance, and medical fields. We recommend developing a framework that incorporates multiple agents working together, which includes a score agent that calculates reliability scores for the model and aids in selecting high reliability data for training. A discussion of possible agent architectures and performance improvements through optimization techniques is also included. Our proposed framework demonstrated superior results compared to current methods in both classification and regression tasks. Additionally, our methodology is applicable to a wide range of data sets with minimal adjustments required. Our method has the benefit of quickly adapting to new data and significantly improving model performance in limited sample size scenarios. Several potential pathways for future enhancements on our proposed framework are also explored. Our code is publicly available for review and use. We believe this framework has the potential for broad application in any setting where model reliability is essential. However, there is a lack of advanced research in this field due in part by the limited availability of high-quality training datasets. In this study, a novel dataset named High-quality X-ray Prohibited Items (HX-PI) is presented which contains a comprehensive collection of high-quality images of prohibited items such as explosives, firearms, and hazardous substances. This dataset of 50,000 images is distinct from previously used artificial datasets or low-quality real-world datasets. In order to enhance the accuracy of prohibited items detection, a Lateral Inhibition Module is proposed which leverages spatial constraints to extract meaningful features from x-ray images, extract regulatory items' features with domain knowledge, and enforce boundaries to prevent the mixture of items' features. Experimental results show that the proposed module achieves superior performance when compared to state-of-the-art general-purpose detection algorithms. Furthermore, this research places emphasis on the significance of domain knowledge in prohibited items detection and presents a method for domain adaptation through the use of high-quality training datasets with varied scales and colors. This approach is then applied to real-world scenarios with satisfying results. Source code and dataset are available at: https://github.com/ChenHongXu19/HX-PI-net.
