The discovery of top quark production in proton-proton collisions by the LHC has established top quark production as a vital benchmark process. Given the larger mass and heavy nature of heavy ions, top quark production in proton-nucleus collisions is expected to be suppressed due to gluon shadowing and anti-shadowing effects, primarily influenced by the mass of the heavy ion. As a result, top quark production in proton-nucleus collisions offers a key test for quantum chromodynamics within the heavy-ion environment of the LHC. Furthermore, top quark pair production can decay into distinct final states, offering various channels for detection, including all-baseline channels, which do not involve the decay of a W or Higgs boson. A thorough investigation of the sensitivity of the ATLAS detector at the LHC to an irreducible background as well as all-baseline top quark production processes has been conducted, with the aim of developing a method for identifying top quark production in proton-nucleus collisions. Additionally, a statistical analysis based on 700 inverse picobarns of integrated luminosity and 3000 top quark pair events has allowed for the derivation of upper limits on production cross-sections in all-baseline channels and top quark pair events in general, with the finding that these limits are significantly below existing proton-proton collision results. Furthermore, with the current detection capabilities, upper limits on production cross-sections in specific final states have been determined to be in the range of 0.68 to 0.88 nanobarns. Furthermore, studies have shown that with further integration of 13 TeV proton-proton data, a significance of 3.3 sigma could be achieved after 700 inverse picobarns of integrated luminosity. The achievement of this level of sensitivity could lead to the detection of top quark production in proton-nucleus collisions at the LHC with a 5 sigma level of significance, which could occur in 2023 with 3-4 TeV proton-proton data following the full implementation of the High-Luminosity LHC. A supplementary analysis has also been conducted to evaluate the performance of top quark and W boson identification algorithms in the presence of heavy-ion background conditions, with the finding that the standard proton-proton selection criteria can be applied to proton-nucleus collisions without modification. A key aspect of this research has involved the development of a novel method for calculating the selection efficiency of top quark pair production events based on the shape of the charge

This study focuses on decoding table schemas and values from semantic formats known as SQL semantics. To enhance the quality of these outputs, we've developed a novel cross-domain framework that learns from both formatted SQL outputs and semantic formats. The model incorporates auxiliary tasks, including a sequence-to-sequence task that produces SQL strings and a format-aware task that predicts specific format markers. By learning from these additional objectives, it achieved superior performance on the F1 score compared to a baseline model. Furthermore, our analysis revealed that the auxiliary tasks facilitate the selection of relevant table columns by capturing the meanings of certain syntax elements. The code for this project has been made available on GitHub. Overall, our paper contributes a framework that successfully executes cross-domain text-to-SQL tasks and provides insights that can be applied to other format-aware interpretation tasks. By using a set of control points to create a parametric road design, we define a driving task that an equipped vehicle must perform. Modifying the control points significantly impacts the road's overall shape and layout. Our approach leverages optimization techniques to identify a set of control points that creates challenging driving conditions, causing the vehicle to veer off its intended path. We validated our method with three distinct search configurations, focusing on balancing testing speed and practicality for simulated evaluations of autonomous lane-keeping systems. Our approach and associated data are now available online for use in researching the limits of autonomous lane-keeping technology. Furthermore, we discuss the potential expansion of our method to design networks from basic shapes, such as circles, to create more diverse challenging driving scenarios. By automating this process, researchers can quickly generate large datasets tailored to testing the limits of autonomous lane-keeping systems, without the need for explicit definition of problematic areas. Our analysis showed that our method can produce high-quality results, even with relatively simple searches, that significantly reduce the necessary computational time compared to other approaches. Temporal action detection is focused on pinpointing the exact start and end times of actions within a video. A key challenge lies in existing boundary matching methods that exhaustively evaluate all possible combinations of start and end times but fail to capture the long-term context. Moreover, densely generated proposals with adjacent semantics do not improve semantic distinctness. To address this issue, we present a new approach called Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN) for producing high-quality action proposals through end-to-end proposal generation, where we incorporate contextual information at both action boundary and proposal levels. For action boundary detection, we employ Multi-Path Temporal Context Aggregation (MTCA) for context aggregation and accurate boundary assessment, while Coarse-to-fine Matching (CFM) is used for context aggregation and matching refinement at the proposal level. Our method has achieved exceptional performance on ActivityNet v1.3 and THUMOS-14, achieving an average mean average precision (mAP) of 35.39% and 54.14% mean average precision at intersection over union 0.5 respectively, solidifying DCAN as a top-performing method. The long-lived palm tree modes (PTM) found in the JET tokamak's edge plasma remain somewhat enigmatic despite detailed documentation. A recently investigated explanation suggests that these structures form when magnetic field eddies caused by edge-localized modes trigger the development of a PTM seed island. However, this study instead seeks to provide an alternate explanation based on observations of edge plasma turbulence. A distinct feature of plasma turbulence is the existence of persistent structures known as blobs and holes in the scrape-off-layer. Measuring the currents within these coherent regions has shown that they follow the direction of the magnetic field. Here, the relationship between these turbulent filaments is likened to ELM filaments, which comprise 'blobs' with enhanced plasma density and interspersing 'holes'. To further this theory, a computer model simulating current within a q=3 surface has shown magnetic fluctuation similarities to those detected by JET in-vessel coils. This implies that the manifestation of a PTM is closely linked to capturing 'holes' on such a surface post-ELM, producing corresponding signatures in magnetic field readings. Conversely, the detection of 'blobs' captured on a q=4 surface would produce the signature indicative of an outer mode, a variant of PTMs. A distinction must be drawn, however, between these outer modes and the more robust PTMs, which involve current within a q=4 surface that is significantly more pronounced. A key factor influencing the formation of these structures is thought to be the timing of the ELM, as tardy ELMs increase the likelihood of 'holes' being trapped on a q=4 surface, while premature ELMs make it more likely for 'blobs' to be captured in such a case. Recent studies on the 64Ni nucleus with a low-spin structure have provided significant insights: combining data from four experiments allowed researchers to identify several 0+ and 2+ excited states below 4.5 MeV, and characterize their properties. According to theoretical analysis, the ground and first-excited 0+ states in 64Ni are uniquely fascinating, as they display a pattern of shape coexistence. Specifically, the ground state 0+ configuration is primarily composed of a prolate deformed shape in rotation, while the first-excited 0+ state, located at 2413.9 keV, is dominated by a spherical shape. Interestingly, the collective 2+ states in 64Ni also show similar separation patterns, with the ground state collective 2+ state arising from a combination of prolate and oblate shapes, and the first-excited collective 2+ state (located at 2760.3 keV) resulting from a spherical shape in rotation. To further understand these findings, researchers performed a theoretical analysis using the Monte Carlo shell model, and found that the intricate structures observed in 64Ni can be explained by the interplay of monopole corrections and zero-spin pairing forces. According to this analysis, the first-excited 0+ state in 64Ni becomes more stable due to the effect of these corrections, while the spherical 2+ state in rotation is favored over its collective 2+ counterpart by a difference of approximately 347 keV. This unique phenomenon is thought to occur because the positive nature of this correction forces 64Ni to prefer the spherical shape in rotation, thus providing a clear proof of the importance of pairing forces in nuclear physics. Furthermore, this evidence can be used to support the development of new interaction forces in shell model calculations. Additionally, 64Ni offers promising prospects for further study, as researchers explore potential connections between its structure and that of 62Co, a nucleus that also exhibits shape coexistence. To this end, they performed a comparative analysis of 64Ni and 62Co using the Monte Carlo shell model, and found that while both nuclei share many structural features, they also display distinct differences, mainly due to the effect of filling incomplete shells in 62Co, which forces this nucleus to select one shape over the other, thus favoring a particular spin state over another. By focusing on the critical point of jamming, they establish a framework for understanding shear thickening as a transition driven by particle collisions, and demonstrate that the critical exponent associated with these collisions matches the prediction of theory for frictionless particles, albeit with some deviation due to an anisotropic contribution that influences shear. By applying this framework to various materials, researchers have generated a plot that graphically represents the anisotropy of multiple systems, and have used it to make predictions about the behavior of materials at their shear-thickening transitions. Furthermore, researchers have investigated the impact of changing variables on the anisotropy plot, particularly with regard to variables that govern the physics of shear thickening, and have demonstrated that anisotropy undergoes significant changes as a result of varying density, while less influential results show that changes in the type of particle or surface chemistry also produce notable effects. Nonetheless, researchers have found that despite these changes, the overall behavior of dense systems remains similar, and that the critical point of jamming serves as a common benchmark for understanding the physics behind shear thickening in these systems. Lastly, researchers propose a new method for determining the anisotropy of systems by using a technique that combines analysis with simulation, and have applied this method to a variety of materials, including cornstarch in glycerol, tantalum nanoparticles in air, and silica particles in glycerol, olive oil, and water. Additionally, researchers have investigated the effects of changing variables on these systems using simulation, and have demonstrated that these effects result in significant changes to the anisotropy of the systems. Lastly, a diagram is provided that graphically represents the anisotropy of these systems. This study supplements our previous research on WIMP-nucleus interaction events in 3D space. Initially, we established a mathematical model describing the velocity of nucleuses hit by Weakly Interacting Massive Particles, specifically considering their scalar and vector interactions. We then examined how the recoil angle distribution of nucleuses changes in response to varying incident velocities, which in turn influence the scalar and vector components. Our analysis revealed that the velocity barrier limiting detection has an unexpected effect on the recoil angle distribution, unlike its straightforward impact on the energy spectrum. Furthermore, our research shows that for incident velocities below the barrier, the recoil angle distribution is parabolically shaped, whereas it becomes asymmetric at higher velocities. This asymmetry originates from the velocity component tangent to the scattering plane, which becomes significant enough to influence the angle distribution. Our investigation also provides a practical method for predicting the recoil angle distribution at any given velocity. Additionally, we derived an expression for the energy spectrum in terms of the recoil angle, which may be useful in interpreting experimental data or setting limits on WIMPs. This formulation explicitly displays the relationship between the energy spectrum and recoil angle distribution. If the latter exhibits an anomalous component beyond theoretical models, such as a cutoff, it could imply the existence of multiple WIMP populations or an alternative source of scattering events. Our research also identifies a critical link between the energy spectrum and recoil angle distribution, which holds significant importance for determining the effectiveness of nuclear detection methods in identifying WIMPs. We analyze two crucial scenarios: one in which the incident velocity is sufficient to generate scattering but not recoil, and another where it has enough momentum to cause either scattering or recoil. An area where Google's impact is most visible is in how people gather information for research purposes. To investigate the effect of Google's influence, we examined how academic database search results are affected when researchers use Google to identify relevant information sources. A survey of information science professionals yielded the results of our inquiry. We discovered a significant discrepancy between the information they found through Google and what actually appears in academic databases. Up to 62% of information considered relevant by the searchers may be hidden from view due to Google's influence. We also discovered that Google's impact varies based on the source being searched, the type of search being conducted, and the characteristics of the searcher themselves. Moreover, we found that searchers are often unaware of the limitations imposed by Google's algorithms and the potential biases that influence their search results. We propose a concept called "viewable relevance" to capture the effect Google has on search results and the implications it has for how effectively information sources are identified. We believe this idea is crucial not just for academic settings but also for other scenarios where Google's influence is likely needed. We encourage researchers and developers to take this concept into consideration and consider our findings, which provide a starting point for further exploration. We plan to expand on this research by collecting more detailed data on search behavior and the effectiveness of search algorithms. We hope this study will prompt developers to reevaluate their approach to designing search algorithms that can identify relevant information sources more effectively. A novel approach is proposed to create and assess a respiratory motion-corrected four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence, which is crucial in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. Data acquisition is continuous via a spiral acquisition method with reordering of Cartesian sampling points (rCASPR) that ensures matching image contrast across different phases. By incorporating a dynamic respiratory signal into image reconstruction, this method prevents blurring caused by respiratory movement. In mock scanner simulations, high-quality images are obtained for large anatomical structures, including the abdomen, thighs, arms, and chest, with minimal residual blurring and accurate phase registration. Additionally, this method is tested on an actual MRI scanner, resulting in clear and well-defined images for comparison with traditional methods. Furthermore, it is discovered that incorporating respiratory information during reconstruction significantly improves image sharpness and clarity, especially in regions with softer tissue types. In mock scanner simulations, peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) values range from 36.8 (upper arms) to 125.6 (thighs), while corresponding structural similarity index measurement (SSIM) values range from 0.80 (upper arms) to 0.99 (thighs). In actual scanner tests, PSNR and SSIM values range from 28.5 (upper arms) to 109.6, and 0.83 (upper arms) to 0.98, respectively. With potential applications in cancer diagnosis, treatment planning, and monitoring, this method demonstrates the effectiveness of respiratory signal utilization in MRI image reconstruction. Experimental data processed via this method is made publicly available for research purposes. In actual scanner tests, reconstruction time takes approximately  5 minutes for 11 phases and 512^3 volume dimensions, with a spatial resolution of 4mm^3. However, a common issue arises when comparing multiple metrics, as typical practices often overlook important limitations and accuracy requirements. In contrast, this paper proposes a rigorous approach to identifying significant differences by limiting type I errors and enhancing type II errors without a specific threshold. Our proposed method has been successfully applied to numerous datasets across four diverse tasks, revealing notable advances over the status quo. In particular, we observed a type I error rate as low as 0.0002 and a type II error rate as high as 0.2531. Our code is available for review and replication at https://github.com/arkadiy/pp-test. In addition, we have introduced a new open-source tool called significant-test, which enables NLP systems to determine statistical significance by calculating the precise paired-permutation test results. Our research has underscored the importance of conducting a thorough type of test, as NLP systems are inherently prone to overestimation due to factors like systematic biases, data selection, and classification difficulties. As a result, we have implemented additional type of test corrections, including the selection of a suitable pause value, type of test, and test power. Our findings have revealed striking variations across different datasets, highlighting the need for further type of test research, particularly in cases where type of test fails to detect a difference or produces an unsatisfactory result. This definition is applicable to volume-preserving area measures and reveals a crucial property: if a surface has a non-empty loom area, it necessarily corresponds to a veering surface. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a surface's loom area or veering triangulation can be determined from its symplectic area measure. This determination process involves identifying critical leaves as geodesic beta-wedges' boundaries, which in turn allows us to recover the veering triangulation through measures' geometric properties. Additionally, we establish a direct connection between a surface's loom areas and its veering triangulation, especially highlighting the relationship between 2-tuples of geodesic beta-wedges and veering triangles. Building upon this connection, we define a surface's "minimal loom structure" as the smallest loom structure containing all of its geodesic beta-wedges. Consequently, we show that a surface's minimal loom structure or veering triangulation can be computed from its symplectic area measure. This computation's success relies heavily on our earlier findings, specifically the fact that a surface's critical leaves correspond to boundaries of geodesic beta-wedges. As a result, we are able to prove that a surface's minimal loom structure or veering triangulation is unique and well-defined. A well-known dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. However, the CountSketch sketch falls short in situations where the querying vectors rely on feedback from previous queries. In such scenarios, the classic estimator can be manipulated by vectors that appear halfway through the querying process and later combine their squared magnitudes. Notably, the CountSketch sketch suffers from this shortcoming even under relatively mild assumptions. In order to address this limitation, we introduce a novel statistical query model, known as the'strong semi-adaptive' setting, characterized by estimators that maintain a minimum 'distance' from previous queries throughout the adaptation process. Within this framework, we establish a CountSketch sketch that successfully identifies the top elements of a given vector with a reduced dimensionality of only $k$ (compared to prior work which requires $k^2$). In addition, its analysis yields a simplified 'large sketch' theorem with broad applications, including the creation of more effective linear estimators for regressing a single element of a given vector. Finally, we discuss a general framework known as 'weak adaptive' inputs, which implies a CountSketch sketch with $n=\tilde O(k^3)$ dimensions sufficient for identifying the top elements of a given vector, and we introduce a concrete example from linear regression that falls within this category. Nonetheless, research into the'strong adaptive' setting remains an open issue. This deformation preserves features like Ahlfors regularity, Poincare inequality validity, and tangent cones with positive scalar curvature. In Part II, we employ surgery-style arguments to successfully remove the singular sets present in these geometries. As a result, we obtain a decomposition of the original manifold into a union of its non-singular parts, along with the removed singular sets. Each of these singular sets, when considered in isolation, exhibits characteristics similar to the reduced geometries described in Part I. Consequently, the removed sets themselves demonstrate regularity properties, thus ensuring they are rectifiable. Consequently, the original manifold can be expressed as the union of its non-singular parts and the singular sets it contains, with the added singular sets being defined by their tangency cones with positive scalar curvature. This outcome holds particular significance in the context of three-dimensional manifolds. As an additional outcome, we demonstrate that a manifold's singular sets can be partitioned into geodesic balls that are conformally deformable, given that the manifold itself is conformally deformable. This achievement leverages analysis and the use of optimal transportation methods to model the evolution of a manifold's geometry. Ultimately, we are able to utilize these insights to successfully prove the Gruenstein-Li theorem. This theorem states that a manifold's singular sets, when defined by their tangency cones with positive scalar curvature, possess a specific characteristic: they are defined by a collection of sets, each of which is a ball with a radius that is directly proportional to its distance from a specific point. This proportion is a constant that is determined by the manifold's geometry in a specific way. This constant, in turn, is a key component in the study's resolution, as it is what ultimately allows the Gruenstein-Li theorem to be proved. This theorem has a significant implication: it means that a manifold's singular sets, when defined by their tangency cones with positive scalar curvature, are actually quite simple in their structure. This simplicity has important consequences, as it means that the manifold itself is composed of parts that are each uniquely defined by their geometry. Initially, we consider the Standard Model Effective Field Theory up to dimension-five operators, addressing questions regarding the scope of New Physics within the Standard Model and whether New Physics can be detected through double Higgs production. Next, we examine the Standard Model Effective Field Theory with New Physics Scales, exploring the reach of such colliders for New Physics Scales below 1 TeV. Finally, we compare the sensitivity of electron-positron colliders to New Physics in the Higgs sector with that of proton colliders, highlighting the distinct advantages of electron-positron colliders in studying the Higgs self-coupling. Optimized cuts and kinematical considerations are accounted for in this analysis. For CLIC, with an available luminosity of 1 ab^-1 at 3 TeV, we find the exclusion limit for the dimensionless Standard Model Effective Field Theory New Physics Coefficient to be around 0.01 at a mass scale of 1 TeV. For ILC, with an available luminosity of 8 ab^-1 at 1 TeV, we estimate a corresponding limit of around 0.1 at a mass scale of 1 TeV. We also predict that ILC can determine the ratio of the trilinear to bilinear Higgs couplings to a 10\% accuracy at 1 TeV, regardless of the underlying theory. Over the years, the availability of Linked Data has surged exponentially with more than 10,000 online datasets now available and formatted according to Linked Data standards, enabling seamless machine readability and interconnectivity.  While such datasets provide numerous opportunities, numerous applications remain hindered due to data of poor quality, significantly affecting tasks such as data integration, search, and interlinking.  Existing quality assessment techniques for Linked Data, although limited, suffer from decreased effectiveness with rising data sizes and become unmanageable for single-machine operations.  To address these challenges, our proposed DistQualityEvaluation is an open-source, cluster-enabled implementation designed for comprehensive quality assessment of large-scale RDF datasets, leveraging the processing capabilities of Apache Spark to distribute quality metrics computation.  This innovative, distributed in-memory approach allows for flexible metric extension via a provided quality evaluation pattern and, through seamless integration with the SANSA framework, has been successfully applied in at least three external use cases, showcasing its superiority over existing methodologies.  Compared to state-of-the-art closed-source, industrial-strength solutions, our system has achieved comparable results with much simpler configuration, reducing evaluation time by up to 5.5 times for certain datasets.  As a scalable and modular system suitable for large datasets, DistQualityEvaluation has been made available on GitHub under an permissive license.  Recent advancements in this project involve a rewritten Spark-based implementation and a corresponding use case, both now integral components of the repository.  Despite its effectiveness, this system has a known limitation - it is not optimized for memory-constrained environments due to the use of in-memory data processing.  As a result, significant performance benefits could be obtained with a disk-based implementation, particularly in such settings.  As this project has been developed as an open research initiative, all community members are invited to collaborate and contribute their own quality evaluation metrics for consideration.  With at least three external use cases already integrating this system and its methods, we have also established a public online forum for all community members to share their own quality assessment results and data, thus further enabling the development of more robust quality assessment algorithms.  As this reference implementation continues to evolve, we have introduced a quality assessment benchmark suite, available for download, to facilitate the assessment of various quality evaluation algorithms against established community standards.  This benchmark includes a total of 8 diverse datasets, each with its own set of associated facts and corresponding truth sets, thus providing a comprehensive framework for evaluating the effectiveness of different quality assessment techniques. This includes single high-mass star formation and binary formations of two massive stars. Our models specifically focus on low-metallicity environments. Two scenarios were explored: one addressing dust particle growth and another addressing the impact of pre-existing dust particles. In the first scenario, dust growth led to a significant reduction in gas absorption at ultraviolet wavelengths and a minor reduction in gas emission at infrared wavelengths. Additionally, it resulted in a relatively small increase in dust mass. However, this increase was insufficient compared to observations following a massive star explosion. In the second scenario, pre-existing dust particles played a crucial role in supplying the observed dust mass before the supernova occurrence. This led to an substantial decrease in gas emission at infrared wavelengths and a significant increase in dust emission at infrared wavelengths following the supernova. Furthermore, it caused a notable reduction in gas absorption at ultraviolet wavelengths and an increase in dust mass comparable to observed values following a massive star explosion. This includes specific masses associated with low-metallicity environments, such as the Cygnus X-Sagitta complex. Our models also identified potential multi-wavelength signatures of dust particle growth and dust coverage, including infrared dust emission, far-infrared continuum, and molecular gas line spectra. Detecting three-dimensional objects at great distances, or far-field detection, is a crucial capability for self-driving cars and remote surveillance systems. However, existing evaluation benchmarks and methodologies focus primarily on medium- and near-field detection. To assess the performance of algorithms in far-field conditions, we introduce Far3Det, a new benchmark based on the P3D network, to measure their three-dimensional object detection skills. To address the challenge of limited annotated data in far-field scenarios, we incorporated a large number of unannotated images from various traffic scenes and applied a technique called few-shot annotation. As a result, we were able to expand the far-field dataset to which we could apply a leading traffic scene dataset, demonstrating the efficacy of our approach through rigorous evaluations and comparisons. Finally, we discovered that far-field detection poses a significant challenge for current algorithms and observed a notable performance disparity between them in far-field conditions. To address this issue, we proposed a simple modification to the P3Det network and successfully applied it, achieving a notable improvement in accuracy. Our work lays the groundwork for advancing far-field detection through the expansion of existing datasets and the development of more robust detection algorithms. We are proud to present the Far3Det benchmark, along with our annotated datasets and code, for the benefit of the community. To build upon our findings, we invite researchers to participate in the Far3Det Challenge 2022, with the goal of sharing their approaches and outcomes. With the growing need for algorithms capable of detecting objects in far-field scenarios, we believe it is essential to prioritize the development of more accurate and robust detection algorithms in this area. To achieve this, we must expand and refine the evaluation benchmarks and datasets used to assess these algorithms, incorporating feedback from real-world applications and incorporating the expertise of experienced engineers in the field. By following this approach, we can ensure the development of more effective and practical solutions that address the complexities of traffic scenes and meet the expectations of industry professionals and the broader research community. Our work on the Far3Det benchmark and the Far3Det Challenge 2022 represents a significant step in this direction, setting the stage for the further refinement of traffic scene understanding algorithms in the future. To facilitate this progress, we emphasize the importance of transparent evaluation protocols and the free exchange of ideas and data within the research community. With this mindset, we hope to contribute to the ongoing development of more accurate and robust detection algorithms in far-field scenarios and to establish a precedent for similar challenges in the field. To achieve this, surgeons need accurate information about the tumor's location and composition, which can be obtained through the alignment of pre-operative medical images with intra-operative surface data acquired from ultrasound or optical sources. This connection leads to prime value existence for a broader class of polynomial sums. Currently, Linux kernel code manually implements system call filtering using Allowlists or Blocklists, which can be error-prone and ineffective. Our method leverages the Linux kernel'seal4virtualization (KASLR) and Address Space Identifier (ASID) features to safely isolate time windows of system call activity and associate them with predicted policy outputs. During operation, Timeloops dynamically generates these time windows and uses machine learning to predict policy settings, eliminating the need for static filtering rules. Our research focuses on optimizing system call density and accuracy of predictions, achieving results with minimal feature engineering. We integrate Timeloops into the Linux kernel and conduct performance tests, showing it can handle a range of workloads while maintaining low latency and throughput. Our results suggest Timeloops has considerable potential as a solution for dynamic system call filtering. We have presented the results from the AstroSat analysis of the high-mass X-ray binary X-ray transient IGR J19294+1816 during its Type-I outburst in October 2019. Timing and spectral data from the decline phase of the outburst revealed the presence of a minute-scale Quasi Periodic Oscillation and a significant Cyclotron Line, with a energy value of 42.7 keV, characterized by a full width at half maximum of 2.3 keV. Additionally, their respective identities were confirmed through broad band spectral fitting, with the Spectral Index showing a relationship with the NHR energy value, which in turn correlated with the Cyclotron Line energy during the decay phase of the outburst. This discovery is particularly significant as it has successfully extended the observation of a minute-scale QPO and a superposed Cyclotron Line in X-ray binaries to the 21st Century. Further studies are necessary to unearthing the underlying physics that govern these phenomena and their possible link to each other. 

Note: Previously, IGR J19294+1816 was reported to exhibit a minute-scale QPO and a Cyclotron Line in 2008, during the decline phase of a Type-I outburst, with a line energy valued at approximately 41.7 keV.

Recent advances in neural speech generation have primarily focused on developing highly realizable and versatile models. One way to achieve this is by utilizing masking strategies to leverage contextual information. Experimental results show that the proposed MaskedSpeech model outperforms baseline models and matches state-of-the-art unconditional speech synthesis systems in terms of naturalness. Furthermore, we found that masked-inference speeches are preferred over direct generation in terms of coherence and fluency. The strengths of MaskedSpeech include its ability to produce diverse outputs and prevent overreliance on straightforward text-to-speech methods. This approach involves utilizing a specific type of van Hove singularity, known as an extraordinary one, which is categorized based on its spatial separation from the Fermi level in complex-dimensional Hamiltonians. Using numerical and analytical methods, a team of researchers led by study leaders K. Seo and I. M. Khayal discovered that extraordinary van Hove singularities can induce significant and persistent pseudogaps in the density of states of multiple Fermion flavors, even at high lattice fillings. In dynamics, identifying new existing attractors is crucial, however, determining unseen attractors within a given equation is an even more difficult task. Here, we present a novel mathematical approach based on resonance theory, which allows us to find all possible coexisting attractors in a wide range of multivariable systems undergoing periodic and chaotic phenomena. By applying this approach, we successfully discovered multiple unseen coexisting attractors in renowned systems, such as the Rossler and Lotka-Volterra equations, and observed how an insufficient number of variables can conceal these attractors. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these hidden attractors can emerge from a specific combination of the system's parameters and dynamics, which we refer to as the'resonant portfolio'. Building upon our findings, we developed an efficient algorithm to accurately identify these resonant portfolios, even in systems with a large number of variables. Ultimately, our research enables the discovery of multiple unseen coexisting attractors in multivariable systems undergoing periodic and chaotic phenomena. Additionally, we explore the implications of our findings in fields such as physics, chemistry, biology, economics, and climate studies, where complex systems often exhibit periodic and chaotic behaviors. Furthermore, we discuss how our results can inform policy-making in these fields and provide opportunities for further research in dynamics and data analysis. Specifically, our studies offer insights into how to control multivariable systems involving periodic and chaotic phenomena and the development of novel nonlinear prediction algorithms. On a methodological note, we introduce an unprecedented high-order Taylor approximation method for predicting periodic solutions and demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation. Building upon our research, we answer an open question regarding the systems in which complete synchronization occurs and uncover novel chaotic patterns in the Bazylikowski-Lenstra-Lovasz localization problem. Moreover, we investigate the complex dynamics that arise from the interaction of first and second order phase transitions in systems undergoing periodic phenomena and uncover novel coexisting attractors in systems studied in the context of coupled oscillators and the dynamics of the planar three-body problem. Finally, we demonstrate how our approach can be applied to adapt the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation to fit experimental data from a stellar convection experiment and showcase the performance of our algorithm using numerical computations and graphical visualizations. On the theoretical front, we generalize our approach to analyze multivariable systems undergoing periodic, chaotic, and mixed phenomena and provide novel proofs for the existence of odd coexisting attractors in systems with odd symmetries and the existence of multiple coexisting attractors

Evaluating the performance of estimators at a single data point is crucial, as it aids in selecting the best estimator for future data sets. Yet, traditional metrics like mean squared error have limitations, particularly for non-normal data. The mean absolute deviation, being a robust alternative, can be an effective evaluation metric. However, estimating the median absolute deviation is complex due to the necessity of controlling bias and variance, as well as coping with the uncertainty inherent in limited samples. A new bias-corrected estimator for the median absolute deviation is proposed, taking into consideration the impact of outlier-sensitive measures and the structure of the data distribution. Through extensive simulations, the bias-corrected estimator is shown to outperform existing alternatives, showcasing its capability to strike a balance between bias and variance in a variety of scenarios. The proposed estimator exhibits particular advantages when estimating the standard deviation and the interquartile range. The theoretical framework provides bounds on the bias and variance of the estimator, while its accuracy is demonstrated through specific applications to real data sets. The new estimator is made available open-source for users to test and integrate into their own projects. The extensive simulation trials, along with the code for the bias-corrected estimator, can be found on the GitHub repository https://github.com/statstat/MDAEC. The bias-corrected estimator offers enhanced performance across a range of scenarios and data sets, positions the median absolute deviation as a superior performance metric, and facilitates the use of this metric in frequentist settings. The name "MDAEC" serves as an acronym for both "Median Absolute Deviation Estimator" and "Mean Absolute Deviation Estimator," capturing the underlying principles of a frequentist approach and the influence of maximum likelihood estimation. The new estimator provides a clear path to the selection of frequentist estimators and serves as a demonstration of the benefits of open-source community review. A comprehensive analysis has been conducted to measure the radii of 3467 young stellar clusters in 31 nearby galaxies, utilizing data from the Hubble Source Catalog and a customized analysis tool. The cluster radius measurements were obtained through a method that compares cluster brightness to the expected brightness within a certain radius, taking into account the effects of mass and age. The radius findings range from approximately 0.5 pc to 7.5 pc, with a median value of 1.4 pc. Notably, a distinct correlation was identified between cluster radius and age, with smaller radii associated with younger clusters and older clusters exhibiting larger radii. This relationship holds true across various mass ranges. The study also discovers a significant correlation between cluster radius and mass at older ages, with a slope of 0.25±0.04, indicating that more massive older clusters tend to have larger radii. Conversely, younger clusters with higher masses do not display a similar increase in size. The study's results contribute to a larger dataset that may be used to investigate the evolution of stellar clusters throughout galaxies. A paper featuring these findings has been submitted to The Astronomical Journal. Meanwhile, a related study on the cluster-radius-mass-age relationship has been accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal Letters. In an example calculation, we apply this approach to $\eta_c\rightarrow 2\gamma$.

precise understanding of the systematic uncertainties in the indirect method. In

In this study, we examine the relationship between boolean structures and involutions within the context of a monoid. Specifically, we investigate the condition under which a boolean structure is uniquely determined by an element's involvement in a set of involutions. This condition is encapsulated by the phrase "involutions form a boolean structure". We then proceed to explore various properties and implications of this condition, applying it to contexts such as sheaves and monoid automata. We also establish an equivalent form for the condition or its negation, expressed in terms of the existence or non-existence of specific paths within a particular graph structure. This equivalence serves as a basis for exploring additional aspects of the condition and its negation, including their interaction with rational functions and language acceptance. A significant aspect of our investigation involves identifying conditions under which the condition or its negation is preserved across substructures, as well as determining the minimal size that a structure can exhibit while still satisfying the condition or its negation. These findings are further illustrated through examples of boolean structures associated with gliding vector automata and counter automata. We also introduce the term "boolean condition" to describe conditions that are equivalent to or imply the condition or its negation, and we explore how these conditions relate to monoid recognition, language equivalence, and other key properties. These advances contribute significantly to our understanding of boolean structures and their connections to involutions within monoid theory. Finally, we introduce an open problem related to boolean structures and their connection to cyclic and anti-cyclic elements in a monoid. This problem has implications for our understanding of boolean structures and their relation to cyclic and anti-cyclic elements within a monoid. We also provide additional context and background information on monoid theory, boolean structures, and related areas through a comprehensive survey of existing research. We applied an innovative approach to study the composition of 34,410 stars in the Milky Way disk using data from the APOGEE-2. The study involved using a binary mixture model to analyze absorption line data for each star, a method that yields two unknowns: the metal content and the abundance of an additional element varying among the stars. We developed a distinct technique to determine the iron content by comparing the measurement from the model to the value derived from a different set of line data. Both methods produced comparable results in terms of sensitivity to physical properties and chemistry. The comparison showed the binary model method to be more precise in assessing iron content, while a study involving artificial stars demonstrated that the APOGEE data can accurately determine the iron content to within 0.05 dex and the abundance of the additional element to 0.20 dex. The model was used to identify five distinct populations within the Milky Way disk based on their chemical content, and the results were compared to previous findings from the APOGEE consortium. The study also revealed a previously unseen population characterized by low metal and carbon content, located 7 kiloparsecs from the Sun. The findings from the study, specifically the distribution of the two main populations in the galaxy, are consistent with an idealized model predicting that the sun lies near a transition border in the galaxy. The study also demonstrated how the binary model can be applied to study the composition of multiple elements in the galaxy. The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant. We introduce a novel loss function variation mechanism that enables neural networks to determine the optimal loss function for a given task by starting from a given loss function and gradually adjusting it through a process of competitive learning. We test this idea using a dataset of loss functions, identifying patterns that indicate certain loss functions are task-invariant, while others are dependent on specific features. We demonstrate that the novel loss function variation mechanism can identify optimal loss functions for a given task and compare it to alternative methods, revealing it yields superior outcomes, while also analyzing the results in the context of the patterns identified. We make the dataset of loss functions, featuring 42 diverse loss functions, along with our code and additional data, available for download at the specified link. We conclude by exploring potential applications for the dataset and future research directions centered on the topic. We believe this research will pave the way for the development of adaptive neural networks capable of selecting the optimal loss function for a given task. In addition, it highlights potential use cases for both loss function variation methods and our research findings in both the machine learning and signal processing communities. Furthermore, we anticipate this study will serve as a starting point for further exploration into loss function variation methods compared to traditional fixed loss functions, leading to potential breakthroughs in both areas. We anticipate our research will also contribute to the expansion of neural network capabilities, enabling them to process a broader range of data types, such as binary data, while allowing them to be trained using a more flexible range of optimization algorithms, including those that utilize gradient information. One significant issue in robotics learning from feedback is the limited nature of demonstrations and corrections given the significant costs associated with making physical changes. Online learning algorithms typically require frequent corrections and can be vulnerable to noisy or misleading feedback. In contrast, we focus on algorithms that can learn from rare, accurate, and timely feedback corrections, incorporating prior knowledge about tasks, processes, and systems. We investigate the performance of these algorithms in complex robotic settings, particularly in tasks involving manipulation and navigation, and assess their effectiveness when compared to traditional online learning methods. Our findings reveal that these algorithms facilitate robust learning on limited high-quality feedback, surpassing the performance of methods not designed for such conditions, and highlight the significance of selecting features that minimize noise and variability when modeling system dynamics. We also observe the ability of these algorithms to be adaptable to new situations and discover that some can be prone to over-correction, a dynamic that could be mitigated by incorporating additional information from past corrections. While several methods for extracting and removing rain from images have been developed, these approaches suffer from a key limitation: they only address part of the problem. Our proposed method uniquely addresses this issue by combining two tasks - creating synthetic rain images and removing real rain from images - and achieves impressive results on both accounts. We integrate a novel technique called disentangled image translation, which involves using generative adversarial networks to translate real rain images into synthetic ones and real images into rain-free versions. This approach enables us to extract a pure rain component by subtracting the dry image from the real image and using a disentangled translation metric. We further refine this process by introducing a disentangled translation metric for both rain creation and removal, which involves using two separate metrics. This strategy allows us to use a single model to remove real rain from images by mimicking a batch of synthetic rain images. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by applying it to both light and heavy rain scenarios and comparing its results to other top-performing methods. We conjecture that this capability enables our model to produce highly realistic rain images. Large-scale scientific computations involving complex matrices often employ a computationally expensive operation called matrix inversion. Despite the cost, researchers have found it to be crucial for various applications such as linear system solving, optimization, and matrix curvature-based optimization. Given the limitations of current Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) hardware, implementing exact matrix inversion via quantum processing units (QPU) is not feasible. However, our research finds that using a hybrid classical-quantum approach, known as the HHL algorithm, can lead to significant portfolio enhancements on NISQ hardware. By evaluating the performance of HHL on various matrix datasets, we found that only a small percentage of the matrices benefit from quantum processing, indicating a opportunities for optimizing portfolio allocation across different problem dimensions. To overcome this challenge, we developed the NISQ-HHL framework that leverages the strengths of both classical and quantum processing, allowing for dynamic decision-making based on the performance of individual matrix dimensions. Through extensive testing on various dataset combinations, we found that NISQ-HHL leads to an average improvement of 2.13 in the quantum roofline model, achieving this gain by significantly reducing the quantum gate count while maintaining a minimal overhead in classical processing. Furthermore, we observed that NISQ-HHL can tolerate an increase of up to two orders of magnitude in quantum error rates before becoming unstable. By utilizing a mock dataset based on a realistic matrix market, as well as actual dataset from the MIMIC-CT Scan collection, we found that NISQ-HHL can produce up to a 5.68x performance improvement and a 5.09x reduction in quantum gate count, respectively. Through dynamic decision-making and optimized portfolio allocation, applications such as linear programming, semidefinite programming, and matrix curvature-based optimization can achieve significant performance improvements, up to 10.15x, on near-term quantum hardware. Additionally, we discovered that NISQ-HHL can also mitigate the need for heavy quantum gate count, allowing for potential applications in machine learning, chemistry simulation, and material science, even with current NISQ hardware, resulting in an overall improvement of up to 8.11x. Furthermore, we found that NISQ-HHL can provide performance gains for different number of QPU units, achieving up to a 10.15x improvement with 1024 QPU units, and we anticipate this performance gain to increase with larger-scale quantum processors. To enhance data efficiency of state-of-the-art end-to-end ASR models and enable them to handle a large amount of unpaired text data through multi-modal training, it's essential to address two challenges: selecting relevant text data and accurately predicting speech. Existing methods focusing on relevant text data usually apply a mask mechanism to ignore unnecessary text information, whereas our proposed approach utilizes a novel bidirectional attention mechanism that allows both text-to-speech and speech-to-text attention to refine each other. By incorporating a speech-guided text encoder and a text-driven speech decoder, our approach leverages the richness of text and speech data. Key advantages of our approach include: (1) learning speech and text representations simultaneously, (2) improving speech recognition by leveraging vast amounts of unpaired text data, (3) enabling multi-modal pre-training and few-shot ASR, and (4) accommodating bidirectional attention through the use of two simple transformers. Experimental ASR results validate the effectiveness of our approach in achieving state-of-the-art performance on various datasets. For example, our method achieves a word error rate (WER) of 1.73% on the 1000-shot Librispeech evaluation set, surpassing the existing state-of-the-art literature by a significant 0.13%. Furthermore, our approach achieves a much lower WER of 5.38% on the 50-shot dataset. Experimental ASR results also demonstrate the importance of both speech-to-text and text-to-speech attention in achieving optimal performance. Additionally, our approach shows great potential in applying bidirectional attention to other multi-modal tasks such as vision-to-speech and speech-to-vision transfer. This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$ for the total variation distance and slower than $n$ for the Kolmogorov distance, this asymptotic behavior is shown, thereby extending previous findings by Diaconis and Hicks. Furthermore, this work also derives rate bounds and statistical limit theorems for the sum or the maximum of the first $k_n$ parking locations. Our main approach to achieving these results is by utilizing conditioned random walk reformulations. Additionally, our investigation into the specific case where $k_n$ equals $\sqrt{n}$ reveals convergent alternatives. This research is a culmination of earlier works by Diaconis and Hicks.

Quantum chromodynamics enables the representation of structure functions as sums over intermediate states of virtual photons scattering off protons made of quarks and gluons.  Using the properties of the quark-gluon plasma in medium, specifically its virtuality and non-zero chemical potential, we relaunch these sums as an integration over the quark-gluon plasma's structure functions.  We then examine the limits of large virtuality and zero chemical potential to reconnect with established results.  Furthermore, our approach offers a framework for interpreting measurements of structure functions as an incisive probe of the quark-gluon plasma.  In the case of deep virtual meson production, our formalism is linked to the isospin decomposition of transition amplitudes, a connection that holds universally across different targets. The Southern Atlantic rift system, extending from 3°S to 37°S latitude, developed as a linear intra-continental rift within the South American and African plates. It formed as a result of the separation of these plates during the Gondwana supercontinent's break-up in the Jurassic and Cretaceous periods. Studies have long been debated over whether this rift system underwent extensional and strike-slip deformation, with some models suggesting it experienced rotation-related extension and narrowing. However, recent magnetic anomalies and seafloor spreads obtained from bathymetric surveys allow for a more precise kinematic analysis of this rift system. Data indicate that the South American plate moved northwards relative to the African plate at 1-2 cm/yr, with no significant component of slip. Additionally, the Antarctic circle's influence caused seasonal variation in ocean and sea-floor spreading rates along the rift's central and southern segments, respectively. These rate variations resulted in distinct sw-NE to sw-SE directed extensional strains across the Rio Grande Rise and Discovery Banks fragments. It is also observed that the South American plate's northerly movement caused the Walvis Ridge and the Discovery Banks to experience right-lateral shear. However, the coherence of these hypotheticals is often checked in isolation, neglecting the fact that coherent phrases often arise from complex structures of nested dependencies within a sentence. To address this limitation, we introduce the concept of phrasal hypotheticals and propose the Disco framework to automatically evaluate the coherence of these constructs at the sentence level. Furthermore, we establish the Disco Coherence Task, a systematic approach to assessing the coherence of phrases and their interconnections within a sentence, and gather a comprehensive dataset named Disco Phrasals, consisting of 12,000 text pairs derived from the Gigaword Corpus. The performance of large language models in the Disco Coherence Task is evaluated, and our results reveal that these models excel in the task but often produce inconsistent outcomes on actual sentences, highlighting the necessity for further research in aligning model performance with real-world applications. To facilitate progress in this area, we welcome contributions from the community in the form of new models, techniques, and analyses. Additionally, we introduce the Disco Phrasals Challenge, aimed at discovering methods capable of producing coherent phrasal hypotheticals from a given context. Any proposed solutions should be evaluated on the Disco Phrasals dataset and assessed for their ability to generate coherent outcomes in the Disco Coherence Task. In recognition of the challenge's difficulty, we are offering a total award of $50,000 to any solution that achieves a score of at least 45 on the 3000-test Disco Phrasals dataset. The source of gamma-rays from nearby galaxies emitting high-energy radiation remains unclear.  Hadronic radiation from the disks around supermassive black holes in these galaxies has been a suggested explanation but is hampered by a problem: it requires significant gas availability in these disks despite their restricted magnetic field making gas escape difficult.  In a new study, researchers examine the possibility that hadronic radiation could result from restricted disks causing local high-energy radiation fields that accelerate cosmic rays or from limited access to cool gas allowing more abundant molecular gas to radiate directly.  Using data from gamma-ray telescopes and molecular gas observations, they find that nearby galaxies emitting high-energy radiation have significant molecular gas availability in their centers and show that this correlation holds true even when controlling for potential contaminants and biases.  Additionally, they find that the gamma-ray emission in these galaxies correlates with the availability of molecular gas rather than the estimated total gas supply, suggesting that hadronic radiation may dominate over direct molecular gas radiation. In contrast, in situations where there are invisible obstructions, the associated gamma-rays originate from wider disks rather than jets and the lack of clear jet structures in these situations may be attributed to a lack of jet collimation or a lack of sufficient magnetic field restrictions in these areas, resulting in broad jet patterns that cannot be detected. Academic researchers who read research papers usually do so to stay informed, but often face the challenge of determining which claims are new and which existing knowledge they reaffirm. To assist in comprehending the content of research papers, sophisticated systems that combine both information retrieval and natural language generation have been developed, but evaluating their effectiveness can be very costly in terms of time and money. Instead of focusing on systems that summarize entire papers, our work centers on developing a dataset that contains question-answer pairs built upon the underlying knowledge, which can be used to evaluate the ability of models to discover relevant information in research papers. This dataset consists of 1112 anchored Q&A pairs, which were created from 300 research papers across three disciplines, and assesses the performance of models that discover knowledge in research papers by evaluating their ability to answer questions accurately. Our investigation shows that both traditional IR-based methods and cutting-edge knowledge-based methods face significant challenges when discovering relevant information in research papers, and that the gap between the best human performance and the best machine performance is substantial. Furthermore, our analysis reveals intriguing insights into the characteristics of both the Q&A pairs and the knowledge discovery task. Additionally, our work highlights the importance of developing more effective methods for discovering relevant information in research papers, which is a crucial component of several critical applications, such as the discovery of relevant sections within papers. In order to facilitate further research into knowledge discovery from research papers, we have created an open-source, publicly accessible repository containing both the anchored Q&A dataset and any new knowledge discovered about research papers. This analysis employs the Majorana equation and focuses on the impact of a linear external potential on the particle's Shannon entropy. Next, we develop an ensemble of Majorana fermions to investigate their thermodynamic behavior. Ultimately, we investigate how both the entropy and thermodynamic properties are affected by the external linear potential. Findings show that in equilibrium, the Majorana fermion's entropy is constant, unaffected by the external linear potential. However, in nonequilibrium scenarios, the entropy's average value increases in proportion to the square of the amplitude of the linear potential. Analysis of the thermodynamic properties reveals a linear relationship between the linear potential and chemical potential. As a result, changes in the linear potential directly minimize the variance of the energy. Consequently, the higher the linear potential, the higher the average energy but also the greater the dispersion. Notably, this relationship holds true for both particle and antiparticle states. We represent the linear potential chemically through the Fermi energy, which follows the formula $E_F = \frac{3}{2}\mu$. With this understanding, we establish a connection between the linear potential and its impact on the Majorana fermion's behavior to analogously infer the effects of a linear external electric field on Dirac fermions. Similarly, we find that, in equilibrium scenarios, the entropy remains constant, unaffected by the external linear electric field. However, in nonequilibrium scenarios, the entropy's average value increases in proportion to the square of the amplitude of the external linear electric field. We conclude that higher external linear potentials may lead to larger variances in energy, potentially outweighing the benefits of increased average energy. This analysis provides a foundation for further investigation into the phenomena arising from linear external potentials and their effects on relativistic fermions. Unfortunately, existing solutions have failed to integrate a comprehensive set of features tailored for both individual users and researchers to explore acronyms across broad categories of texts. To fill this gap, our project introduces MadDog, a cutting-edge, web-based platform tailored for both user-centric and research-focused acronym identification and disambiguation initiatives. By providing an interactive interface for user-defined acronyms and a robust disambiguation algorithm capable of handling multiple definitions for each acronym, MadDog enhances the comprehensibility of acronyms within diverse texts. Furthermore, its innovative technology offers researchers valuable insights into acronym distribution and usage across different text contexts. To demonstrate its capabilities, MadDog includes several datasets comprised of technical articles and patents, along with accompanying analysis and performance evaluations. Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the Hall conductivity. Current research has made notable strides in understanding and replicating topological effects through artificial materials, particularly photonic, phononic crystals, metamaterials, and electrical circuits, centered around Dirac/Weyl points. Conversely, topological nodal lines – one-dimensional singularities in momentum space – are relatively understudied. This review aims to illuminate the theoretical basis of topological nodal lines and outline recent developments using artificial materials, featuring examples of non-Abelian charges observed in nodal lines in momentum space and their realizations in photonic systems. Furthermore, it discusses the challenges associated with both experimental and theoretical investigations of topological nodal lines. Leveraging the unique properties of artificial materials, researchers hope to devise new techniques for the precise observation and manipulation of nodal lines, contributing to a deeper understanding of topological physics. Additionally, this review provides guidance for future research in this field. Finally, it outlines the potential benefits that could arise from integrating concepts of topological nodal lines with other effects, such as interaction between points and lines, enabling the creation of more complex non-trivial systems. This knowledge can be used to develop custom materials with optimized topological properties, making them suitable for a range of applications spanning electronics, optics, and thermodynamics. This, in turn, may lead to breakthroughs in energy production, storage, and conversion, along with advances in medical treatments, with examples including magnetic resonance therapy, drug delivery, and heat management. This complexity further increases with the presence of multiple tumor types within a single scan. To address this challenge, our proposed MAG-Net uses a multi-task attention directed network. This approach allows the network to focus on specific tasks while processing the input data. We also explored the effects of adding auxiliary classification tasks to the training process. Our experiments demonstrated that MAG-Net achieves state-of-the-art performance for multi-task learning and overcomes classification hurdles when applying commonly used image analysis protocols. This technique transforms an interlaced video sequence into a seamless progressive scan video output. We introduce a novel computational approach based on deep learning, which outperforms conventional methods by achieving a higher PSNR score of 1.26 dB and a lower NSSD index of 0.16 compared to existing solutions, while executing at a fast real-time speed of 43 fps using a single GPU. This improved performance is attributed to a modified U-Net architecture, which uses spatial and temporal convolutional layers to capture complex pattern similarities across both progressive and interlaced video sequences. Our model's effectiveness is verified through comprehensive evaluation, testing, and comparison with established methods using diverse video datasets. Ultimately, our research proves the potential for optimized performance, both in terms of speed and accuracy, in various video processing applications. Our code has been made publicly available online. Despite achieving superior results, our model lacks a theoretical explanation, which constitutes an area in need of further research in the field of video restoration. Our study suggests that certain video enhancements can be achieved through the use of single-layer neural networks alone. In contrast to composite networks, single-layer models exhibit several key advantages, including increased flexibility and a more compact design that facilitates easier integration into existing video processing frameworks. This, in turn, raises the question of whether older methods can still provide competitive performance, at least in specific scenarios. This study presents a novel, high-order numerical technique for solving the linear Fokker-Planck equation under a constant diffusion term. The method is developed from a reformulated equation in conservation form and involves a Lagrange-Galerkin approach, utilizing high-order Lagrange polynomials to approximate solutions. Associated stability and convergence analyses are provided, demonstrating that the method maintains its high-order accuracy despite the non-linear source term. The proposed method is particularly useful for modeling mean field games, where it facilitates the computation of systems of Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equations by approximating the unknown potentials through high-order polynomials. Several numerical examples illustrate the method's efficiency and accuracy in solving both scalar FP equations and systems of HJB equations, including cases involving nonlinear advection terms. Custom-made tools have been integrated into the PDELab framework in the MATLAB environment to implement the Lagrange-Galerkin method for linear FP equations. This implementation is made available to the scientific community. Additionally, the recently introduced Theodorou package for solving HJB equations has been modified to incorporate the Lagrange-Galerkin method's high-order approximations of the potential, leading to enhanced accuracy. Our analysis expands on earlier work by Giudici, Li, and Praeger by considering a broader class of 2-(p^k-1)-groups for prime powers p and set p^k = q^m with p > 2. Our findings result in an infinite number of twisted wreath structures from 2-(q^m-1)-groups, leading to an infinite number of locally arc-transitive graphs with a star normal quotient whose automorphism group has a simple subgroup. This research also provides examples of twisted wreath structures whose arc-transitive graphs have a nilpotent automorphism group. Despite its efficiency for handling continuous and categorical variables, the Group Lasso often results in inconsistent estimates, rendering the model difficult to interpret due to the lack of sparsity. To achieve a sparse solution using the Group Lasso, we propose a two-step method: first reducing data dimensions through the Group Lasso, and then employing an information criterion on a subset of clustered models. This algorithm's performance is evaluated under high-dimensional conditions and compared with state-of-the-art methods using synthetic and real-world datasets, showing its superior performance in terms of prediction accuracy and model size. Additionally, our results indicate that consistent estimates can be obtained under specific conditions, making our method a viable solution for sparse modeling. Furthermore, our algorithm's flexibility allows the inclusion of penalty parameters through an alternative method, which is also illustrated using real-world datasets. A novel approach has been developed, allowing these models to be fine-tuned for specific tasks by incorporating structured knowledge from online resources. This article explores how nonlocal diffusion models can be formulated to be consistent with the principles of maximum entropy and maximum relative entropy. We establish a link between these models and the fractional Laplace operator, and demonstrate that they can be derived from variational approaches based on the thin-edge limit of Dirichlet domains in three-dimensional space. This connection provides a framework that can be applied to derive consistent local and fractional limit theories, encompassing stable states, phase transitions, and free boundary problems. Furthermore, this framework enables the investigation of new free boundary problems and phase transition models, which can also be studied through the lens of fractional physics. Specifically, we can examine fractional isoperimetric problems, fractional mean curvature, Capillarity problems, and nonlocal minimal surfaces within this consistent local and fractional limit framework. This work is a compilation of multiple research articles on these topics. In part I, we discuss consistent local and fractional limit frameworks, as well as the formulation of consistent two-material problems for both local and fractional Laplace operators. In part II, we explore free boundary problems and phase transition models, which can be studied through the lens of fractional physics. In part III, we focus on the description of consistent two-material models with mismatched surface tensions, accompanied by a discussion on established results, recent advances, and potential research directions within the field. In part IV, we investigate fractional convergence and nonlocal minimal surfaces, while part V concludes the series by examining fractional isoperimetric problems, mean curvature-type equations, Capillarity problems, and nonlocal minimal surfaces within the consistent local and fractional limit frameworks. This research focuses on identifying minimal sets of features necessary to create a seamless panoramic image, given that certain areas are already well-matched. Initially, we analyzed existing work on panoramic stitching, particularly notable studies by Snavely et al. and Zhang et al. Building on this foundation, this study aims to minimize the number of features required to achieve high-quality results, incorporating the effect of gravity on the selection process. To achieve this, we formulated a method to evaluate the importance of features based on their contribution to maintaining a consistent pose across the image sequence. Subsequently, we implemented a strategy to select the most critical features through non-maximum suppression, followed by a validation process to ensure the chosen features produce a reliable and aesthetically pleasing outcome. Experimental results revealed that our proposed method yields substantial reductions in feature counts while maintaining comparable performance to state-of-the-art techniques in terms of visual quality and accuracy. Furthermore, we observed our method to be particularly effective at eliminating redundant features in image sequences featuring prominent vertical obstacles. To facilitate replication and assessment, the source code and data sets used in this study are available for download. Moreover, we explored the applicability of our proposed approach to mobile robot vision applications by conducting a series of experiments, with the findings also included in the supplementary material available online. Overall, this study contributes a novel algorithm for efficient feature selection in panoramic image processing, with potential extensions to compute vision-based gravity directions and applications in mobile robot vision systems.
