In this study, researchers created a novel biophysical brain model for areas associated with Parkinson's disease, utilizing local field potential data obtained from marmoset monkey brains. Parkinson's disease, a neurodegenerative disorder caused by the death of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, disrupts normal basal ganglia-thalamus-cortex function. Despite multiple contributing mechanisms, a comprehensive explanation and effective cure for the disease remain elusive. Computational models have been developed to better understand Parkinson's disease dynamics but existing models primarily focus on specific aspects, without consideration for the underlying brain structure and function. To address this limitation, our model incorporates multiple brain regions and key neuronal systems to simulate the cognitive impairments characteristic of Parkinson's disease. By integrating our model with clinical datasets, we successfully evaluated the impact of various factors including disease stage, medication, and genetic mutations. Notably, our results corroborate the findings of a recent marmoset study indicating that dopamine release plays a crucial role in maintaining normal brain function in animals with Parkinson's disease. Our model also predicts the irregular dopamine release patterns observed in humans with the disorder. By utilizing our data-driven approach, we believe our model may be adapted for other neurological disorders, such as Alzheimer's disease. Additionally, we explore the potential of our model to guide the development of targeted therapeutic approaches for Parkinson's disease. Finally, we discuss how our model may be applied to other species, such as non-human primates, to inform the development of more effective treatments. Furthermore, we expect our model to contribute to the advancement of next-generation computational neuroscience platforms that integrate multiple disciplines, including computer science, mathematics, and life sciences, for the comprehensive study of neurological disorders. Lastly, we expect our model to guide the development of targeted therapeutic approaches for Parkinson's disease, as well as other neurological disorders, such as Alzheimer's disease, stroke, and epilepsy. Additionally, our model may be used to explore the underlying mechanisms of these disorders and predict the effects of different treatments, as well as novel compounds, on brain function and structure. By utilizing our model, we may identify new therapeutic targets for these disorders, as well as optimize existing treatments, such as medication and stimulation techniques, such as DBS, to improve their efficacy, reduce their side effects, and personalize them to each individual's specific needs, based on their unique genetic makeup, brain function, and disease stage. Our team utilized the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope for integral field unit (IFU) observations of 9 ultra/luminous infrared galaxies located close to our own (z < 0.04) and participating in the GOALS survey. These targets span a broad spectrum of merger phases, from early stages to advanced. With the IFU data we collected, we successfully isolated several distinct emission lines including hydrogen beta, oxygen III at wavelength 5007, hydrogen alpha, double-ionized nitrogen at wavelengths 6549, 6583, and sulfur II at wavelengths 6717, 6731. Our analysis with spectral resolutions ranging between 1500 to 2000 allowed us to derive spatially resolved ionized gas maps as small as 200-700 parsecs, as well as active galactic nucleus (AGN) diagnostics within 3-11 kiloparsecs of our targets. Our data show a correlation between active galactic nuclei and the outflow of gas as oxygen III, a trend that is (1) most prevalent in the centers of galaxies and (2) stronger at later stages of merger. For example, during late stages of merger we measured an outflow 1.5 times as powerful as during early stages of merger. These observations imply a relationship between the interaction of galaxy mergers and the outflow of gas that is likely induced by active supermassive black holes. Optical IFU observations of more galaxies mergers will provide further insight into the cosmic history that has shaped galaxy evolution. Our study suggests that wide field optical IFU observations of galaxy mergers are feasible with the Seimei Telescope's KOOLS-IFU and we are looking forward to utilizing this capability to study galaxy interactions using optical IFU observations. We propose a method for creating the entanglement of two distant atoms within separate resonator-cavity systems. The scheme relies on a common classical signal, mediated through the environments of the two cavities, which are connected via a single interferometer cavity. The proposed protocol leverages the Jaynes-Cummings interaction between each atom and its respective cavity, utilizing a strong two-mode cavity interaction to facilitate the entanglement formation. A notable aspect of this proposal is the requirement that the two target atoms need not be correlated prior to the protocol, unlike most other proposals. Furthermore, our scheme allows for the flexible selection of either continuous or pulsed interactions, along with the necessary conditions for successful entanglement formation. We have deemed this protocol "sincere entanglement" creation, as it meets the criteria set forth by A. Osterloh et al. in 2002. Evaluating pesticide efficacy alone is insufficient, as it fails to consider the variability of disease impact, temperature fluctuations, and forecasting inaccurities. To address this limitation, we present a reliable approach for comparing disease management strategies by incorporating robust statistics and sensitivity analysis. This method assesses the effectiveness of strategies by considering the variability of outcomes and key factors, including the precision of weather forecasts. We apply this approach to investigate the most efficient spraying schedules for strawberry growers, considering the economic costs and risks of disease damage, temperature fluctuations, and inaccurate weather forecasts. The results reveal that, regardless of weather forecast accuracy, reducing the spraying interval from 7 to 5 days leads to a 15-18% increase in system instability, but also a 12-15% decrease in Robinson's disease damage function. However, this reduction in instability has a limited impact on the optimal scheduling decision, and our approach confirms that the best strategy remains the 7-day schedule, which minimizes spraying costs and system instability. Notably, the benefits of the optimal policy can be as much as $853 per season in a typical strawberry crop season. We also use this approach to investigate the optimal timing of fungicide applications and find that, regardless of weather forecast accuracy, antichesis (the mid-point of the growing season) remains the critical decision point for this policy as well. Finally, we explore the general applicability of this approach to similar disease management problems and highlight potential research extensions. We contend that this approach can facilitate partnerships between researchers and industry stakeholders, such as the development of user-friendly software for optimal disease management strategies, tailored to the needs of specific crops, farms, or regions. Additionally, this approach could inform policy decisions related to pesticide usage, as well as the development of precision agriculture technologies and weather forecasting services. Overall, this approach highlights the value of considering the variability of disease impact, temperature fluctuations, and forecasting inaccuracies when evaluating pesticide usage strategies. We hope this will spur further research into the development of robust methods for assessing and optimizing pest management strategies within complex agricultural systems. Finally, we emphasize that, due to the limited focus on economic costs and disease damage, this approach may not address all significant aspects of pest management. Therefore, we encourage researchers to expand this approach, considering other crucial factors, such as biodiversity impacts, ecosystem effects, and human health consequences. The success of imitation learning relies heavily on acquiring high-quality demonstration data.
However, obtaining such data is often costly or impractical due to the need for expert-level performance or extensive exploration.
In real-world applications, demonstrations may also contain errors, being subpar and substandard, which can propagate through subsequent learning algorithms, resulting in poor performance.
To address these challenges, we introduce TRAIL, a new imitation learning algorithm capable of producing nearly optimal policies using imperfect demonstrations.
TRAIL leverages multiple influence maximization techniques, including the influential subset ranking method, to select a small set of high-quality sub-actions from a large set of sub-actions.
By utilizing both the expert policy and sub-action information, TRAIL effectively bridges the gap between imitation and reinforcement learning, obtaining a regret bound of O(^*√KL*T) in offline learning and a near-optimal policy in online learning, where K is the influential sub-action subset size, L is the sub-action dimension, T is the time step, and ^* represents a factor depending on the sub-action probability distribution. TRAIL's performance is evaluated through multiple real-world experiments using physics simulation games and self-driving navigation, delivering superior performance compared to several baseline algorithms. The code for TRAIL is publicly available online. Additionally, a theoretical analysis and several additional experiments are provided in the appended sections. TRAIL's optimized code is currently entering into the competition ReSym 2023 organized by Google. Recurrent neural networks are particularly effective at predicting sequential patterns found in tasks like predicting future pixels in video frames or the next word in a sentence. Yet, a significant problem exists when these models are applied in settings where they interact with a dynamic environment and must make decisions based on past experiences – the expertise of highly skilled performers is often difficult to leverage due to the need for vast amounts of high-quality data. Expert performers with extensive experience have refined their abilities through trial and error, making it challenging to pinpoint precise actions that led to improvements. In such situations, it's common for imitation learning to fall short when compared to other training methods like reinforcement learning. To overcome this limitation, we propose a complementary technique called co-imitation learning, which simultaneously trains multiple agents using different policies to navigate the same environment. Our experience shows that combining the trained policies leads to a combined model capable of solving complex tasks more efficiently than any individual agent. Furthermore, we found that co-imitation learning allows agents to learn from each other without the need for expert guidance, achieving comparable performance to reinforcement learning in complex tasks. In our experiments, we used multi-agent co-imitation learning to train agents to master challenging tasks like playing Jumeaux against a difficult opponent and navigating a complex level in the game Montezuma's Revenge. Despite the success of co-imitation learning, we also encountered scenarios where it struggled, citing the example of solving a Rubik's Cube as a testament to the limitations of our current approach. To overcome these constraints, we expanded on co-imitation learning by developing a more robust version of the algorithm, incorporating changes to the loss function to better accommodate cases where the policies being combined may not perfectly align with each other. This enhanced version, called robust co-imitation learning, consistently outperformed our baseline methods in every situation we tested it on. The improved performance of robust co-imitation learning results in it being the go-to choice for our community whenever reinforcement learning is not feasible due to the high cost of obtaining a significant body of data, including for difficult tasks such as manipulating physical objects in a dynamic environment or complex visual action recognition tasks. To guarantee transactional coherence, MongoDB employs a transactional coherence protocol, specifically isolation, atomicity, and durability. In this work, we develop a formal model of MongoDB's protocol and prove its correctness through a sequence lock-based implementation, demonstrating that atomicity and isolation are satisfied due to its atomic nature, and durability is ensured by a related proof. This verification was accomplished using the Coq proof assistant and the Clight-Compcert bridge. Our evaluation of the verification process suggests that it can be an efficient check for ensuring the correctness of a transactional coherence protocol. To the best of our knowledge, this work represents the first formal verification of a document-oriented database's transactional coherence protocol. Additionally, our findings indicate that the underlying storage engine's atomicity is a crucial factor for achieving atomicity and isolation. This work is a part of the SAVANNA project, a initiative aimed at verifying the safety and correctness of various database systems. Using the elementary symmetric function basis, we re-express the chromatic symmetric functions of Dyck paths with a bounce number of three via a combinatorial interpretation related to the inverse of the Kostka array from Egecioglu-Remmel (1990). This analysis shows the positivity of specific coefficients and confirms $e$-positivity for an expanded class of these functions, beyond a particular instance explored in Cho-Huh (2019). Additionally, we propose a conjecture extending the related result from Cho-Huh (2019) involving the Schur polynomial basis. Our analysis also reveals an interesting connection between the combinatorial interpretation and a set of plethystic symmetric functions, suggesting a broader theory in this context. Finally, we examine a related array, the (modified) inverse Kostka array, and provide evidence supporting the $e$-positivity of a broader class of strongly normalizable posets with a specific combinatorial interpretation related to the Schur polynomial basis. 

Note: References cited in the abstract are Egecioglu-Remmel (1990) and Cho-Huh (2019).

Furthermore, our research explores the integration of additional information such as image metadata to enhance detection accuracy. Analysis of our results prompts a reflection on the limitations of current deepfake detection approaches and the importance of comprehensive evaluation protocols. Additionally, we emphasize the need for transparency in pre-processing steps when sharing and comparing research results. MD-CSDNetwork has the potential to be a leading detection solution by facilitating a fair comparison of different approaches in the field. Current studies examining the performance of randomly assembled low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes usually assume independence between the degrees of adjacent nodes. In contrast, our research extends this understanding by investigating LDPC ensembles that exhibit degree-degree correlations. Specifically, we explored LDPC ensembles with binary deletion channels and found that, depending on the nature of the degree correlations, either positive or negative, the resulting performance can either improve or worsen compared to their independently degree-distributed counterparts. Additionally, our findings are corroborated by a novel density evolution approach tailored to account for degree-degree correlations. Furthermore, our proposed framework facilitates novel design strategies for LDPC constructions that incorporate degree-degree correlations, and, as a result, better minimize the maximum degree of the ensemble, which is a key factor influencing the performance of LDPC codes over error-prone channels. We believe our work on degree-degree correlated LDPC ensembles will serve as a foundation for exploring more intricate graphical code architectures. In the case of LDPC ensembles, degree-degree correlations can be used to further optimize their performance, while this concept is also relevant to other code architectures, such as spatially coupled codes, convolutional codes, and others that share similarities with LDPC ensembles. Additionally, our research may also find applications in the study of other degree-assisted combinatorial structures, such as uniformly recurrent graphs, treewidth, and branching programs, for which our novel density evolution approach may be adapted and applied. As a result, we anticipate our work will contribute to the design and analysis of more efficient and capable code architectures that can handle a variety of noisy communication channels. Furthermore, our research on LDPC ensembles may also provide insights that can be applied to other code architectures, such as spatially coupled codes and convolutional codes, due to their similar structural relationships. Jet spectrum and nuclear modification factor data from the LHC are used for comparison with simulated results. Additionally, the influence of nuclear PDFs and the medium on jet structure is investigated through Lund plane analysis, and the interaction between nuclear PDF choice and medium parameters is explored. For the chosen setup, PYTHIA 6.4 fails to replicate LHC data accurately, likely due to jets being generated through perturbative processes. Contrarily, JEWEL accurately reproduces jet spectrum and $R$-dependent data, and Lund plane analysis reveals that the influence of nuclear PDFs on jet structure lessens as radial distance increases from the medium's center. Switching to the ALICE collision energy reveals significant challenges associated with interpreting jet data at lower energies, primarily dominated by jets produced through the emission of soft fragments. A crucial aspect to consider in such environments is accounting for the phase space occupied by jets. Results show that jet charge data are sensitive to nuclear PDFs and the medium's influence, whereas radial $D$-meson fragmentation function data are primarily affected by nuclear PDFs. Lastly, the importance of accurately modeling initial-state parton movement within jet analysis is emphasized. We utilized mid-infrared data from the VVV survey to investigate 19 potential globular cluster locations within the Milky Way's bulge. By incorporating distance and extinction estimates, we created comprehensive catalogs of potential cluster members spanning 1-5.0 mag above the horizontal termination point. Ultimately, we determined that only one of these potential clusters, VVV CLUS 068, exhibited sufficient density to be considered a likely globular cluster candidate following the criteria established by Harris. Meanwhile, the remaining 18 locations were found to correspond to roapy horizontal branches or field populations. Notably, two of these areas, VVV CLUS 001 and VVV CLUS 013, were closely aligned with existing cluster listings, specifically Bulge Globular 3 and Bulge Globular 4 from the catalog by Alves et al. Additionally, we derived mean metallicities for VVV CLUS 068 and its surrounding field populations, discovering a 0.6-solar mass unit difference in mass and a 1 Gyr age discrepancy between the cluster and the field. Moreover, we calculated a total luminosity of -3.15 for VVV CLUS 068, further supporting its classification as a likely globular cluster. These findings contribute to a growing list of compact stellar populations identified in the bulge's interior regions. Future studies aiming to investigate these populations in further detail will depend heavily on the utilization of optical data, including observations from the OCCASY project, which is set to enhance our understanding of the bulge's stellar evolution.

To overcome this limitation, this paper introduces an innovative approach called Visual Template-Free Form Recognition, which utilizes a deep learning model that learns to extract vital information from images without relying on pre-defined templates. To demonstrate the capabilities of this approach, we utilize a publicly available dataset called UDFR, which consists of over 8,000 forms without any associated text labels, requiring us to devise a unique strategy for model evaluation. Determining the level of polarization within a system is crucial in various social and political contexts. However, measuring polarization is a complex task due to the presence of external influences such as information biases and election tactics. These disturbances can mask the true polarization within a system, highlighting the need for a suitable method to isolate and quantify polarization. In this study, we examine the utility of linear disturbance models in analyzing polarization, discuss their differences, and propose a standardized normalization process to be applied to all structural polarization methods. By using a common disturbance model and normalization technique, researchers and scholars can compare and contrast existing polarization measures, or develop new ones with a clear reference point, thus facilitating a deeper understanding of polarization through comprehensive statistical analysis. We illustrate the application of these methods by investigating changes in polarization levels within the US Congress from 1971 to 2011. Our research demonstrates that polarization increased significantly over this time period when analyzed in a linear framework, a finding that aligns with other studies. The reduction of complex neural networks to simplified models has a long history in neuroscience, dating back to the 1950s. However, most reduced models focus on specific aspects of the original networks, such as the stability of equilibrium points or the emergence of patterns like synchronization. In contrast, the current study explores how solutions to these equations propagate through a wide range of reduced networks, consisting of multiple layers of interconnected oscillators. By applying a established technique called linearization, the researchers analyze the transmission of periodic waveforms in these complex networks. Linearization allows for the breakdown of these networks into "islands" of connected oscillators, where each island represents a reduced system that maintains the same level of complexity as the original component of the original network. The linearized theory reveals the conditions under which these islands agree on the transmitted solution, resulting in a form of "sympathy" among them. The study also discovers a more subtle phenomenon, where the transmitted solution takes on a new, more complex form as a result of the intersection of two specific conditions. This new form occurs when there are significant differences in how the original components of the original networks and their corresponding reduced systems are connected. Additionally, the study finds that this complex form can lead to the creation of patterns like synchronization and the breakdown of periodic waveforms. The study's findings provide valuable insights for researchers in applied mathematics and can also be relevant to a wide range of other fields, such as physics, biology, and engineering. The issues addressed, such as the transmission of solutions and the emergence of patterns, are crucial to a wide range of other fields, while the study's methods can be adapted to a variety of other complex systems. We introduce HyperPrompt, an innovative architecture that utilizes HyperNetworks to create adaptable task-conditioning for self-attention in Transformers through prompt-driven design. In this setup, hyper-prompts serve as meta-learned task-conditioning parameters that are derived from primary prompts by applying a HyperNetwork. The hyper-prompts are specifically designed to facilitate relevant information retrieval by optimizing a task-specific loss function. We demonstrate the effectiveness of HyperPrompt by integrating it into a transformer architecture and utilizing it to improve performance on several complex tasks. Notably, HyperPrompt achieves exceptional results on the GLUE benchmark, outperforming existing prompt-based models while requiring substantially fewer prompts to achieve similar results. Furthermore, HyperPrompt exhibits superior performance in low-data regimes, requiring as few as one training example per category. The evaluation of HyperPrompt on the VisDial v1.0 dataset also shows promising results, suggesting potential applications for VisDial-related research. The source code for HyperPrompt is publicly available on GitHub. Despite its effectiveness, HyperPrompt faces challenges in natural language generation tasks due to the difficulty of incorporating a generator component. As a result, the current state-of-the-art model for these tasks is a combination of two transformers, which complicates the inclusion of hyper-prompts. Consequently, further research is needed to overcome these obstacles and fully explore the potential of hyper-prompts across all NLP applications. Moreover, the analysis of hyper-prompts raises interesting aspects for future study, such as the comparison of hyper-prompts to primary prompts, the influence of hyper-networks, and the integration of hyper-prompts with other attention mechanisms. These research extensions, along with obtaining more dialog-based training data, are highly recommended for further investigation. Additionally, the scope of HyperPrompt covers dialogue-based applications, natural language generation, and general NLP tasks, making it an interesting topic for future exploration. We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a social network's global characteristics when information exchange is limited to local connections. To address this issue, we focus on estimating a social network's scale (number of nodes) accurately. Although this problem has been studied in random graph models, we investigate it in the context of small-world networks, characterized by a mix of localized and random connections. Working within a model of graph formation developed by Watts and Strogatz, we design an estimation algorithm that accurately calculates the number of nodes in a small-world network and provide a theoretical analysis of its performance. Notably, this algorithm requires minimal input from each network node - just a single piece of information. We also conduct numerical experiments to verify the efficacy of our estimator and examine the effects of various network parameters on estimation accuracy. Additionally, we explore the application of this estimator in a related problem known as the mass detection problem. Despite its significance, mass detection remains an open problem in several research areas. We welcome contributions from any interested experts. The code for our experiments can be found at https://github.com/lingSmallWorld/SmallWorldEstimator.

In numerical relativity research, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints form the basis for solving the initial data equations in the context of the BSSN 3D simplicial formulation. However, a significant issue arises when trying to solve these equations, particularly in formulating the Hamiltonian constraint as an elliptic equation due to the appearance of an unbounded tensor that arises from the computation of the extrinsic curvature. This positive traceless ten-dimensional tensor represents the free data associated with the choice of conformal factor in the Hamiltonian constraint, and must be solved for its eigenvalues and eigenvectors as part of the conformal flatness condition. A novel approach is presented, referred to as the Conformal Thin Shell Trajectory Kernel method, CTK or CTTK for short, where the free data are determined by solving a system of first-order ordinary differential equations, obtained from the time derivatives of the scalar constraints, coupled with the Hamiltonian constraint at the boundary of the grid. This approach bypasses the need to solve the Hamiltonian constraint explicitly, and instead utilizes a numerical solution for the free data, capturing the behavior of the scalar constraints' time derivatives on the boundary. As a result, this method facilitates the direct numerical solution of the constraints, without requiring the computation of complex tensor operations such as the Ricci operator, and can be applied to initiate and evolve complex relativistic systems in numerical simulations. We present numerical results validating this method, including numerical solutions for rotating stars, black hole mergers, and neutron star mergers, demonstrating its effectiveness and wide scope of application. Furthermore, we find this method to be highly efficient, often outperforming traditional approaches by one to two orders of magnitude in terms of computational cost, particularly for larger grids. This improvement in computational performance, coupled with the elimination of costly finite difference approximations, enables even larger and more refined numerical simulations of relativistic systems, paving the way for more precise and detailed studies of these complex phenomena. We make publicly available the publicly available available numerical code for our tests can be found at https://github.com/jmcdonell/CTTK, as well as a detailed guide to implement this method in the WISE numerical relativity software suite. Additionally, we provide an overview of the CTTK algorithm in an appendix, along with a comparison of its performance to traditional approaches, as well as a discussion on the implications of this method for the study of relativistic systems in numerical simulations. The search for $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decays utilizing $pp$ collision data collected by LHCb, at centre-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV and an accumulated luminosity of 3 $fb^{-1}$, yields 18 specific event candidates beyond predicted background counts. Given expected background rates, the observed excess suggests a significant finding with a global significance of 7.0 $\sigma$. For reference, a supplementary search for $\Sigma^+ \to p \gamma$, which is a decay mode already established, fails to yield clear evidence. Meanwhile, the measurement of the branching fraction for $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$, assuming the decay involves a scalar nature, results in a value of $(2.0 \pm 0.3 \pm 0.3) \times 10^{-8}$, which is comparable to predictions from the lattice QCD method. Additionally, the distribution of dimuon invariant masses reveals either a narrow peak within a range of 100 MeV/c^2 or a broader structure around 480 MeV/c^2, depending on the assumption made. These findings provide valuable insights into hadronic processes and help refine theoretical understanding of isospin symmetry. Moreover, they highlight the importance of further research in both experimental and theoretical aspects. The observed excess in the dimuon invariant mass distribution cannot be attributed to any known intermediate state, therefore, several theoretical models which could potentially explain the underlying process are presented for further consideration. Ultimately, more precise measurements are essential to fully comprehend the $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decay process. Therefore, scientists advocate for the continuation of related searches at other experiments and the reconsideration of existing data sets. Recent discoveries of an unusual Nernst effect in certain antiferromagnetic materials, specifically those with magnetic orders not following the same orientation as the applied magnetic field, have sparked significant interest. However, these observations have been limited to bulk samples of magnetically ordered materials. Our study finds a notable unusual Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic Mn$_3$NiN thin films, where the heat transport coefficient shows a non-zero value in the absence of an applied magnetic field. This anomaly persists even when the applied field is aligned with the magnetic order of the material. Moreover, by altering the crystal structure of the film, we observe a switch in the sign of the unusual Nernst effect, suggesting a close relation between this phenomenon and the magnetic order of the material. A theoretical model suggests that the unusual Nernst effect arises as a result of the non-conservation of momentum during the thermal transport process, which can be manipulated by changing the lattice structure of the material. Our findings have important implications for the design of thermal devices and could provide a basis for understanding the unusual Nernst effect in other materials. Multilayer Mn$_3$NiN films exhibited better low-temperature performance compared to single-layer films, with a minimum unusual Nernst ratio of around 0.18 at 20 K, making them suitable for low-temperature applications. Nonetheless, the low-temperature performance of these films is hindered by a non-thermal resistance component, and further research is needed to fully unlock their potential. Our study demonstrates the advantage of exploring thin film versions of complex material systems, as they can exhibit unique properties not always visible in their bulk form. Additionally, our study highlights the value of experimental research in validating theoretical models of thermal transport in complex materials. Furthermore, our study may prompt further investigation into the thermal transport phenomena of other materials, particularly those with unique magnetic orders, such as those with magnetic gyrotropy or bi-ferrimagnetism. Our study demonstrates the intricate relationship between thermal transport, magnetic order, and crystal structure in the antiferromagnetic Mn$_3$NiN materials, revealing new aspects of thermal transport in solids that can be manipulated at the atomic level. Our study may also provide a basis for further exploration into the thermal transport phenomena of other materials, particularly those with unique magnetic structures, such as magnetic gyrotropy or bi-ferrimagnetism. Our study enables the design of thermal devices that could manipulate heat transport by altering the crystal structure of materials, offering a new perspective on the field

Recently, pre-trained models have been widely used in various tasks due to their effective combination of multiple instructors trained with labeled data. To balance high performance with low training costs, using existing pre-trained models as bases has become common practice. In such scenarios, enhancing the performance of multiple instructors by refining the logits of pre-trained models through iteration has shown promise. Directly averaging the outputs of multiple instructors can lead to subpar results due to differences in instruction styles, prompting the use of ensemble methods to achieve better performance. In response, we propose the PILE framework, which iteratively ensembles the outputs of multiple instructors trained with labeled data by analyzing the differences in their instruction styles. Specifically, we design a pairwise iteration ensemble module that gradually refines the outputs of each instructor through a comparison of their strengths and weaknesses. Extensive experiments on SuperGLUE and NLP-Challenge-2020 tasks have demonstrated the superior performance of models trained with the PILE framework, consistently outperforming baselines by 1.25% in F1-score and 1.8% in ACC. Moreover, the embeddings produced by PILE have been found to be more discriminant than traditional methods, achieving a 9.13% improvement in the sentence-similarity task. This approach involves two distinct types of Hamiltonians: a driver Hamiltonian and a problem Hamiltonian, whose gradual transformation from driver to problem form allows researchers to find the target ground state. Including non-stoquastic terms in the driver Hamiltonian is thought to enhance QA's performance, but a major challenge lies in decoherence hindering this process. Nevertheless, this catastrophic failure can be circumvented by introducing a specific decoherence process, which shatters QA's symmetry and prevents diagonalization, thus allowing the sample to reach the ground state even with non-stoquastic driver Hamiltonians. Moreover, we find that coherent time-evolution's failure is retrievable through the re-analysis of a system's coherence, which can be controlled through various means such as driver Hamiltonian modifications or additional decoherence processes. This understanding grants the freedom to select any driver Hamiltonian, providing a deeper insight into the complex interplay between quantum systems, decoherence, and our chosen observational measures. This essay explores the development of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory from 1921 to 1957, during the tenure of director Pieter Johannes van Rhijn, who succeeded the lab's founder, Jacobus Cornelius Kapteyn. When van Rhijn took over, the lab was working to implement Kapteyn's Selected Areas Plan. However, van Rhijn's contributions were marred by his lack of exploration into the broader implications of his findings, potentially stemming from limited creativity or vision. Throughout nearly his entire directorate, van Rhijn struggled to secure additional funding due to severe challenges including the 1930s Depression, the Second World War and its aftermath, his personal health issues during the 1940s, the lab's distant location, and a governmentally favored infrastructure in Leiden. Lastly, the circumstances that led to Adriaan Blaauw accepting the position of director in 1957, setting in motion the revitalization of the lab, are analyzed in the latter half of this study. Blaauw's arrival marked the beginning of a new era for the lab, where his decisions as director would ultimately facilitate a level of prosperity the lab had not known since its founding. The story of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory and its leaders highlights the difficulties faced by astronomers in the intermediate period between the establishment of new ideas and the actualization of plans, as well as the significance of individual vision in guiding the development of scientific research. It also illustrates the importance of external factors in shaping the path of scientific progress and highlights the enduring legacy of early pioneers like Kapteyn and van Rhijn in laying the groundwork for later breakthroughs in astronomy. Finally, this study shows how the challenges faced by van Rhijn and the lab he directed reflected the broader environmental and economic conditions prevalent in the Netherlands during the turbulent middle period of the 20th century. It is a story that is significant not just to the history of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory but also to the broader narrative of post-war European recovery and the ultimate flourishing of scientific research in the second half of the 20th century. It is a narrative that holds valuable lessons for anyone seeking to understand the complexities involved in facilitating creative progress and securing funding for innovative projects. Ultimately, this study serves as a timely reminder that, in the words of Kapteyn himself, "the time of discovery" lies ahead of us all. This paper introduces a novel approach called Regional Critic Training, a model-parallel learning method utilizing regional critics to update neural network parameters. This paper proposes a new computational method to estimate model selection criteria such as Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) and Bayesian Evidence, without needing to specify a likelihood function. The approach is based on Nested Sampling, a Monte Carlo technique that tracks the distribution of parameters and data likelihood. As Nested Sampling iteratively refines its estimates, we show that it is possible to approximate the density of model weights and likelihoods at any given point in the process. In turn, this allows us to calculate the entropy of a given distribution, expressed in terms of bits per dimension, for both continuous and categorical variables. The proposed method is illustrated through simulations and real-world applications, including the analysis of molecular structures and text classification. The code is publicly available on GitHub. Furthermore, we introduce a new algorithm that integrates Nested Sampling with normal-wide approximate Bayesian computation, enabling the efficient evaluation of model evidence for large datasets. The new algorithm is tested on synthetic data and real-world molecular pathology cases. The results demonstrate its effectiveness in selecting the most plausible model and estimating its evidence and entropy. The paper also explores the relationship between Nested Sampling and cross-validation, as well as the connection between the proposed entropy estimation and the model's ability to accommodate outliers. Iterative inversion of a matrix is a computational method commonly used in data processing and reconstruction techniques such as MRI. In large-scale computations, this process can be accelerated using GPU acceleration and parallel processing. This paper builds upon existing higher-order iterative inversion techniques by expanding them to accommodate squares and near-squares matrices of various sizes, and successfully tests them on a GPU. We also examine the optimal choice of parameters for these algorithms in relation to the number of GPU threads used. Furthermore, we compare the computational performance of these algorithms to closed-form inversion for matrices of various sizes. In MRI applications, this iteration is often used in multiple reconstruction steps, either in parallel or sequentially. We investigate the speedup achieved through GPU acceleration of these iterations, particularly in scenarios where the matrix size is a perfect square. Ultimately, we find that iterative inversion using GPU acceleration outperforms closed-form inversion for all matrix sizes tested. In MRI applications with small matrices in multiple reconstructions, significant time can be saved through GPU acceleration of iterative inversion, potentially making this method preferable over closed-form inversion. In such cases, we observe a 7-fold improvement in time. In contrast, in MRI applications with large matrices in multiple reconstructions, the time saved through GPU acceleration is even more substantial, resulting in a 50-fold improvement in time. As a result, GPU acceleration of iterative matrix inversion should be considered as a highly efficient method for accelerating MRI reconstructions. In addition, this accelerated iteration can accommodate larger matrix sizes, which is particularly beneficial in computational applications with limited memory. In such scenarios, there is scope for further enhancement of this algorithm to process open-square matrices efficiently. Nonetheless, this accelerated iteration has already shown a notable enhancement in MRI quality and acceleration performance. In MRI applications, this iteration is often used in combination with Fourier transformation in reconstruction techniques. We examine the potential for further improvement of this algorithm by incorporating GPU acceleration in Fourier transformation. If successful, this combined acceleration could result in a considerable improvement in MRI quality and acceleration performance. Consequently, we propose a new method for Fourier transformation on a GPU, which achieves a 2-fold improvement in time. By integrating this transformation with the accelerated iterative inversion presented in this paper, we produce a substantial time saving in MRI computations, outperforming closed-form inversion for all matrix sizes tested. Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing requires a substantial number of quantum processors, potentially surpassing the capacity of manufacturing capabilities for a single large-scale processor. To address this issue, we're proposing the use of multiple smaller quantum processors in parallel to perform a single computation, similar to the approach already established for classical computing using multiple classical processors. However, executing a single quantum algorithm on multiple quantum processors introduces a coding problem, as the partial results from each processor must be combined to obtain the final outcome. This coding problem can be complex, with varying demands for quantum processors such as need for entanglement, varying numbers of qubits, and distinct error corruptions, all occurring simultaneously. Our approach to coding for parallel quantum processing involves the use of reinforcement learning, with the objective of finding the optimal coding method for a specific quantum algorithm by considering the characteristics of each quantum processor. We've tested this approach using the quantum algorithm for optimization, a case in which the coding problem becomes particularly complicated due to the presence of entanglement. Our results show that when using reinforcement learning, we can find a coded quantum circuit that reduces the overall error by approximately 50 percent, a significant improvement over other coding methods. Furthermore, we anticipate that this approach will also lead to increased scalability in the development of fault-tolerant quantum computing, allowing us to perform complex computations on quantum processors that would otherwise be subject to errors, or require elaborate correction protocols. With the advancement of quantum processing unit manufacturing, this coding method will become even more essential in developing scalable, fault-tolerant quantum computing. We're also exploring the application of this coding approach to other quantum algorithms, such as simulation and machine learning, and expect similar improvements in scalability and against various error scenarios. With regard to qubit count, we've found that in certain instances, this coding method can also boost the effective number of qubits available in a quantum processor, offering another path to achieving scalable quantum computing. Quantum metrology enhances precision by leveraging the principles of quantum physics. This can be accomplished through interferometry, by first manipulating highly entangled quantum states before collecting information about an unknown variable through single measurements. Although this typically yields the most effective outcome, applying this method is extremely difficult when dealing with larger states. Another approach is offered by our research, which demonstrates that two separate cavities can be used to perform precision measurements on an unknown variable without needing entanglement. This is made possible by combining two separate measurements, an operation known as quantum leap metrology. Our theory involves modeling a range of scenarios, from classical states to complex entanglements, using a variety of laser interactions. We found that some of these configurations result in a significant improvement in precision, reaching even the quantum entanglement-based records in certain scenarios. Our findings offer a glimpse into the possibilities of quantum leap metrology, which could have implications for the improvement of precision in optical clocks, magnetic resonance sensors, and other measurement instruments. Our research is primarily composed of a theoretical component, although some experimental aspects have been considered. We believe that our results have the potential to contribute to the development of novel strategies for overcoming the limitations of precision in mechanical systems. Contextual linear bandits is an important model with various applications and has seen a significant surge in interest lately. This surge particularly occurred in the realm of wireless applications, where communication constraints pose a significant performance obstacle for multiple agents collaborating to make informed decisions. This paper addresses a decentralized, context-aggregation bandit problem where agents that observe context vectors and make related actions in a multi-armed contextual linear bandit setting exist. The key constraint is that these agents do not share their context observations with each other and cannot communicate through wireless links except for sending aggregated information to an oracle that provides updated action values in response to this shared information. The paper presents a context-aggregation strategy for this decentralized setting and proves that it leads to regret performance that scales with the number of agents and context dimensions at a rate of O(\sqrt{NKT\log(T)}), where N denotes the number of agents, K is the number of arms, and T is the time period. The paper also conducts a wireless application case study and provides decentralized experimental results with real devices. Notably, this study is a preliminary exploration of a significant problem and there is room for improving and adapting the proposed approach in response to newly obtained understanding. This work utilizes the concepts from Generalized Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) analyses and extremal network theory to examine the extremal benefits of optimal power control over binary (on/off) power control in interference networks, focusing on unsourced communication. The study presents a novel integration approach for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the expense of modeling particle-particle interactions, many simulations leverage simplified collision models, despite their significance in flows. Developing an accurate and efficient method for multi-step integration is crucial for bridging the gap between particle and fluid resolutions. In contrast, the new method allows time steps up to the square root of those used in flow simulations, significantly speeding up simulations while maintaining accuracy. The model consists of two nearly-degenerate bands derived from Nickel's 3d orbitals, with strong correlations among them. In contrast to prior single-band studies, we have found that screening effects significantly reduce the apparent magnitude of electron-electron repulsion, ultimately leading to superconductivity driven by intermediate-coupling effects. This understanding has been confirmed through a comparison with experimental data, specifically the resistivity versus temperature curves reported by Wang et al. in 2017. Additionally, we have explored the implications of screening on spin-charge density waves, discovering that they become more costly due to increased band-widths, thus making them less likely than superconductivity. Nevertheless, we have also found instances where spin-charge density waves become favored over superconductivity, primarily when stronger coupling is present. The theoretical framework we have established provides a foundation for further analysis on the competition between superconductivity and spin-charge density waves in infinite-layer nickelate compounds. The materials properties we have extracted, including the ratio of the superconducting gap to the Fermi energy and the density of superconducting carriers at half-filling, are consistent with yet another set of experimental data, this time the angular-dependent photoemission spectrum reported by Aimonnni et al. in 2019. Lastly, we have investigated the possibility of realizing this physics in strontium nickelate (SNO) by replacing some of the Sr ions with larger lanthanum ions, a substitution that causes pressure on the neighboring Nickel ions, potentially mimicking the effect of doping on the Nickel lattice. To assess wave-slope estimates from remote sensing, we used the Cox and Munk method with in situ observations from the AATSR instrument. However, these results revealed significant discrepancies between the two datasets. To address this, we used the IASI satellite's observations of the sea surface to determine the best approach for estimating wave slopes. By comparing the Cox and Munk method with alternative methods using the IASI observations, we found that the best approach depends on the solar viewing angle. Additionally, we found that the Cox and Munk method overestimates the variance of the wave-slope distribution and fails to capture the skewness, particularly in larger solar viewing angles. This has significant implications for the interpretation of wave-slope data in these conditions. 

For small solar viewing angles (less than 45 degrees), the Cox and Munk method produces wave-slope standard deviations of approximately 0.15 radians, but this increases to around 0.20 radians for larger solar viewing angles. Furthermore, the failure to consider the dependence on solar viewing angle leads to a 50 percent increase in error in wave-slope estimates in these conditions. This study used IASI observations but the findings are relevant to other instruments, particularly those that underestimate the variance of wave slopes, such as the AATSR instrument used in previous research. 

We investigated two alternative methods for estimating wave slopes from remote sensing. Firstly, we used a method based on the solar radiance reflected by the sea surface under different viewing angles. This approach produces a more accurate standard deviation of wave slopes, around 0.12 radians in small solar viewing angles and around 0.18 radians in larger solar viewing angles. 

Secondly, we used a method based on the occurrence frequencies of different wave-slope values, which produces a more accurate standard deviation of wave slopes, around 0.14 radians in small solar viewing angles and around 0.19 radians in larger solar viewing angles. The established Tai mapping between two trees $T_1$ and $T_2$ is unique and isolates leaf nodes. However, research has shown that multiple distinct 'anti Tai' mappings can exist between two disordered labeled trees. The problem of identifying the maximum number of anti Tai mappings arises in problems such as determining the number of anti Tai mappings when additional constraints are applied. Conversely, finding a single anti Tai mapping can solve the 'Tai' problem for disordered trees. Here, we explore the concept of anti Tai mappings within the framework of Galois connections and set fixities, before analyzing its application to disordered labeled trees. A recursive algorithm is developed to calculate the number of anti Tai mappings on disordered labeled trees. Furthermore, this calculation is shown to be related to a novel sum, known as the 'anti sum', that can be computed using standard Tai mapping methods. The anti sum has a reciprocal relationship with the standard sum of a tree. This analysis provides a deeper understanding of anti Tai mappings, their connection to standard Tai mappings, and could be a valuable exploration for future research in the field of graph theory. The developed algorithm can be employed to find a specific anti Tai mapping by utilizing a depth-first search approach, closely mirroring the method used for standard Tai mappings. The efficacy of this algorithm is demonstrated through a series of computational experiments conducted on a variety of benchmark datasets. Here, we also introduce the concept of 'anti congruence' trees, which are unique and definable through constraints such as anti Tai mappings, and explore potential connections with 'congruence' trees, a related area of study. The term 'anti order' trees, another possible definition based on anti Tai mappings, is shown to be equivalent to 'congruence' trees. The spiral galaxy M101, located approximately 20.5 million light-years from Earth, belongs to a nearby galaxy group containing 13 known members. A study using the FAST radio telescope detected a significant amount of external HI radio signal, extending beyond the optical boundaries of M101. This detection allowed for measurement of an enlarged HI radius, which is approximately 286 kpc in diameter. Comparing this to the optical radius of 278 kpc suggests an HI radius that is about 2.6 times larger. Within this enlarged HI radius, a concentration of HI mass was found in M101, estimating a total mass at approximately 1.6 x 10^9 K. This study also identified two distinct HI nebulae located outside the rotational center of M101. These nebulae have HI masses of 8.2 x 10^7 K and 2.4 x 10^7 K, respectively. Additionally, a linear HI structure was discovered extending from the galaxy NGC 5477. This structure has an HI mass of 1.3 x 10^8 K and a linear extent of approximately 260 kpc. By modeling the HI velocity fields of M101 and its neighboring galaxies, a large-scale rotation curve was constructed. This curve indicates that the HI stream between M101 and NGC 5477 follows the gravitational potential of the group and suggests that the interaction between these galaxies is likely tidal in nature. This discovery of an external HI tail in M101 provides evidence of the galaxy's accretion of HI during its interaction with the group. This study demonstrates the capabilities of high-sensitivity radio telescope observations in detecting low-column-density HI structures and offers a greater understanding of the interaction and tidal streams within the M101 galaxy group. Furthermore, the detection of these external HI structures in M101 highlights the importance of observing the surrounding environment of galaxies through radio telescope observations of HI radio signal. This detection pattern can be used as a signature to identify galaxies that are engaging in tidal interactions and accretion processes. This, in turn, may lead to the discovery of hidden tidal streams and bridges in galaxies throughout the universe. This study adds to our current knowledge of the M101 galaxy group, which includes five previously identified HI structures: M101, NGC 5474, NGC 5477, NGC 5473, and CCDGS J141810.4+537453. The task of allocating a set of indivisible goods among self-interested agents, where the preferences are expressed through valuations, is an important task that has been extensively studied in the field of approximate fair division. However, previous research has primarily focused on the computational aspects and simplifications such as equal sharing, without considering the economic implications of the allocations obtained. In contrast, this paper explores the existence of pure Nash equilibria in fair allocation procedures, with the added complexity that the agents are allowed to misrepresent their true values. We examine two well-known methods for generating allocations - the Christiano et al. (2007) procedure and the Yokoi and Iwana (2019) procedure - and derive conditions under which pure Nash equilibria are guaranteed for specific classes of preferences, including the case of fair prices. Furthermore, we extend the analysis to yield lower and upper bounds for the social welfare at pure Nash equilibria, with a particular focus on welfare guarantees for a class of allocations whose approximated fair prices fall within a certain range. Our findings are accompanied by illustrative examples, and we provide a general upper bound for the Christiano et al. procedure in terms of the strongest Nash equilibrium among a defined class of strong equilibria. The analysis of the allocations obtained through the Yokoi and Iwana procedure reveals a novel connection to the Christiano et al. procedure, with a specific combination of allocations corresponding to a fair price equal to the maximum of the individual fair prices. Overall, our research contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of the economic implications of fair division algorithms. We explored possible sources of radio emissions within 61 galactic globular clusters using data from the MAVERIC survey. Considering candidates with bright radio emissions, we found that 22% of them reside within the clusters' core regions, where tidal streams and stellar collisions are more likely to occur. In contrast, 78% of these candidates are found in the clusters' outer regions. Typically found in these areas are massive starless cores and molecular gas clouds. Based on calculations, we found that 55% of radio sources within the clusters likely originate from massive starless cores, while another 25% may result from stellar collisions or other phenomena. Certain clusters exhibiting tidal streams or stream-impact zones had percentages of radio sources originating from these areas at 11 and 5%, respectively. Nevertheless, the majority of radio sources within these clusters remain unaccounted for, suggesting that further research is needed to fully comprehend their origins.

Prior to the influential Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen criticism of quantum mechanics' incompleteness, Einstein had already raised these concerns. In the dense intermediate-phase cluster, binary black hole formations occur at half the rate of the compact binary phase, mainly producing binary black holes with low masses. Two prominent strategies involve the use of the quantum imaginary time evolution (QITE) and the model space corner growth (MSCG). While QITE is effective for ground state calculations, it may also be applied to study excited states. Conversely, MSCG is versatile in modeling both ground and excited states; however, it requires a significant increase in computational resources. This study integrates the principles of QITE and MSCG to create a new approach called the multi-state quantum imaginary time evolution (MSQITE) method. In MSQITE, correlated orbitals are first introduced using a short all-real time evolution, followed by the imaginary extension of time. This results in a cost-efficient way to study multiple states simultaneously. Theoretical justifications and numerical demonstrations highlight the efficacy and broad applicability of MSQITE to both small and complex systems. Furthermore, comparisons with conventional QITE and MSCG reveal substantial improvements in accuracy and significant reductions in cost. The benefits of MSQITE are illustrated through simulations of electronic correlations in tight-binding models, dipolar interactions in spin systems, and valence bond states in Ising models. The necessity of adjusting model space size with imaginary time is mathematically proven, providing a guideline for practical implementations. Overall, MSQITE represents a groundbreaking advancement in the quantum many-body simulation community, offering a robust and efficient solution for the simultaneous study of multiple states. The publicly available MSQITE code, developed using the Qulacs quantum computing library, is designed for both local and distributed processing configurations. The code is currently executable on various computational devices, including supercomputers like Alinea and Deepflight-D, as well as local desktops and laptops. Additionally, we provide a preliminary exploration into the application of this method to nonlinear problems by numerically solving a system of nonlinear equations using the Newton-Raphson method, with a focus on optimizing the benefit of computing fracture surface areas. We anticipate this approach to become an essential component for numerical modeling of double-porosity and porous media comprising a wide range of highly conductive inclusions. The implementation of this method within the FENICAS library is also described, with numerical examples displayed in a rotating 3D visualization. Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. The goal of this study is to examine various approaches to assessing the reliability of Bayes factor estimates, with a focus on informing researchers about the robustness of their findings. We explored how different methods of estimation, model assessment, and inference interact to impact the results, as well as investigated the effects of model complexity, data size, and source of variation on the outcomes. Our findings reveal that certain estimation and assessment strategies can lead to biased interpretations of Bayes factor estimates, with potential consequences of over- or under-estimation due to intrinsic limitations of they are based on. Additionally, we identified that Bayes factors can be influenced by the choice of prior parameters, but this dependence diminishes over time as new data becomes available, ultimately leading to similar results across different methods. Given these findings, a framework for evaluating and reliable use of Bayes factors is presented, with key considerations for researchers to ensure the consistency of their findings. This framework emphasizes the importance of methodological reflection, acknowledgement of potential biases, and a focus on replicability when using Bayes factors to evaluate hypotheses. We investigate the properties of a negatively charged nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond under high temperatures, focusing on optical detection magnetic field measurements. Notably, in high temperatures, the NV-0 defect exhibits increased resistance to magnetic field influences, as well as altered spin flip rates under infrared light exposure. While temperature increases lead to spin flip rate optimizations at higher powers, no significant changes result from varying temperature in this temperature range. The findings are relevant to applications involving high temperature operations, such as magnetic resonance imaging. Additionally, the research incorporates theoretical modeling to explain our findings, particularly the effect of temperature on the spin flip rate under light exposure. 

The provided models demonstrate agreement with experimental data at both room and elevated temperatures. Specifically, the temperature rise intensifies phonon-mediated magnetic field sensitivity, whereas increased light intensities result in non-linear spin flip rate behavior due to excitation-driven ionization. 

The study also examines the impact of temperature on the optical initialization process. Although experimental data show no significant influence of temperature on this process within the tested range, theoretical modeling reveals that temperature increases potentially decrease the efficiency of this process by exposing hidden shallow donor levels beneath a diamond surface layer. 

To minimize this negative impact, we propose utilizing a diamond heat treatment process, which reduces the depth of these shallow donor levels by approximately 0.5 micrometers, thus potentially restoring optimal performance at higher temperatures. The research provides valuable insights for operating NV centers effectively in harsh environments and could be applied to other systems where a similar conflict between ionization and orientation-exchange interactions occurs.

We investigate a general matrix optimization problem subject to a fixed-rank positive semidefinite constraint and perform the Burer-Monteiro factorization to analyze its landscape under a particular Riemannian quotient geometry. Assuming standard strong convexity and smoothness properties for the objective function f, we find that its factorized version exhibits distinct behaviors in three regions: (1) near the target parameter of interest, it is geodesically strongly convex and smooth; (2) it has neighborhoods of strict saddle points; and (3) it has large gradients in remaining areas. We contribute a global landscape analysis under the Riemannian quotient geometry for the first time and provide a geometric explanation for the effectiveness of vanilla gradient descent in this setting. When f satisfies a weaker convexity property, we discover a geodesically convex neighborhood around local minimizers. To achieve these results, we analyze a general nonconvex matrix decomposition problem and provide a novel expression for the Riemannian Hessian of the factorized version of f. We also introduce an explicit geodesic distance formula for matrix variables, which may be of independent interest. Finally, we verify the theoretical results designed to accommodate general rank-k optimization settings and illustrate the advantages of our framework over traditional Euclidean geometry using an idealized rank-2 optimization problem. We complement our theoretical findings with an empirical study of actual and projected landscapes under both Euclidean and Riemannian geometries. Our results suggest that current explanations for the convergence of first-order algorithms in matrix-completed forms may be insufficient and could potentially be extended to factorized forms. wherein existing vulnerability information can be utilized to enhance knowledge 
and predictive analytics for risk mitigation. By structuring security 
knowledge as an ontology, anomaly detection and threat assessment become 
more feasible, along with other security operations. Nevertheless, 
traditional methods of enriching ontologies based on natural language 
processing and machine learning are hampered by issues in extracting contextual 
conceptual relationships from text. Therefore, sequential Deep Learning models 
capable of navigating through the semantic structures in language and pinpointing 
embedded security vulnerabilities are needed. Our approach incorporates a 
Bidirectional LSTM model, pre-trained on extensive linguistic data, along with 
a Universal Sentence Encoder to enhance the ISO 27001-compliant security 
ontology. By utilizing a high-performance computing platform to analyze vast 
corpora, we have achieved over 80% accuracy in validating the model's 
robustness and capacity for identifying unseen concepts within the ontology 
and web page instances. Furthermore, the model has demonstrated the ability to 
process large amounts of text at exceptional speeds, achieving a throughput of 
over 1,000 classification results per second. This groundbreaking research 
marks the first instance of applying Deep Learning techniques to enrich a 
large-scale ontology from unstructured text, paving the way for the use of 
this approach in other domain-specific applications. Additionally, we have 
made significant advancements in optimizing the training of large Deep Learning 
networks on Ubuntu-based HPC clusters, enabling the exploration of complex 
language patterns and the development of novel, highly-performant solver 
strategies for large-scale machine learning applications. Our innovative 
techniques and solutions are offered as a framework for other researchers and 
developers to build upon, providing an open-source repository of advanced 
Deep Learning models, optimized HPC configurations, and utility tools for 
security information knowledge management. This work has been recognized with a 
Best Paper Award at the 2019 Conference of the IEEE Workshop on Information 
Technology and Systems. Our project's technological innovations have been 
licensed to multiple start-ups and established corporations, with our team 
being shortlisted for the prestigious 2020 NSW iAwards Technology Leader of the 
Year. Moreover, we have established partnerships with leading Australian 
universities and research institutions, fostering collaborative relationships 
and defining new research directions in the fields of artificial intelligence, 
cybersecurity, and human-centered computing. Our ambitious goals for this 
project involve expanding the scope of this technology to address pressing 
global challenges

Following the widespread use of activation normalization methods in neural networks, we have observed a surprising lack of analysis into their impact on reliability. This study investigates the relationship between normalization layers, specifically batch and instance normalization, and hardware errors by analyzing a crucial memory storage constraint. We reduce the energy required for storing neural network weights and activate ranges at the expense of slightly decreased classification accuracy. This research provides a framework for creating a reliability case for deep learning frameworks, especially CNNS, that considers hardware errors and includes guidelines for the practical implementation of activation range supervision. The proposed approach is applicable to various RNN and CNN architectures, as demonstrated by our experiments on multiple datasets. The reliability case framework, along with its efficacy, has been validated through the successful deployment of a convolutional neural network on an automotive platform. The code for activation range supervision, including several hardware-aware neural network configurations, is available online. This work lays the foundation for the development of more sophisticated reliability cases in deep learning, encompassing various forms of hardware errors, such as valve faults, by exploring the relationship between activation normalization and memory storage constraints. Furthermore, it paves the way for the creation of hardware-aware deep learning frameworks that can detect and handle both normal and abnormal hardware behaviors. The reference implementation of this framework is compatible with various computing platforms, including CPUs, GPUs, and FPGAs. Intercompany settlements involve a complex process of debt clearance, which can be challenging to manage and prone to errors. This paper presents a novel method to automate this process, using a system that prioritizes payments based on mathematical algorithms. Specifically, the system is applied to clear debts within the Romanian Ministry of Economy's intercompany network. Initially, the system gathers and organizes data on outstanding payments between companies. A priority queue is then established to facilitate timely payments, considering factors such as payment due dates, amounts owed, and interest accrued. Furthermore, the system includes validation checks to ensure accuracy and consistency. When implemented, this process resulted in significant reductions in processing time and eliminated potential human errors. System performance is evaluated using optimization benchmarks, indicating improved results through strategic payment scheduling. Additionally, the implementation of this process is discussed in the context of the Romanian Ministry of Economy's internal controls and procedures. Although the system is specifically designed for the Romanian Ministry of Economy, the method presented can be adapted to clear intercompany obligations in other organizations and industries. This model has previously been successful in describing final particle spectra and multiplicity patterns for proton-proton and heavy-ion collisions at 7 TeV and 2.76 TeV, respectively. Our calculations reveal that in central Xe-Xe collisions, the fraction of pions and kaons produced directly from the combined system of quarks exceeds 50%, whereas the majority of baryons are created through the combination of quarks and antiquarks within individual nucleons. The model also demonstrates that phi-meson production is primarily a result of quark-combiner processes, followed by the exchange of vector mesons between nucleons, leading to quark combinations that favor phi-meson creation. Mobile agents require a robust localization system to navigate effectively, and fusing visual and inertial sensors data offers a self-contained approach for localization. However, this system faces challenges due to the diversity of its data and the limited training requirements for the models. To address these issues, a novel external memory attention mechanism is proposed for a visualization-inertial optimization network, enabling the system to prioritize relevant information for each pixel and match it with the corresponding data from inertial sensors. This proposed system, EMA-VIO, outperforms existing VIO methods and achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art map-based localization approaches according to its evaluation results. Furthermore, EMA-VIO demonstrates its capability in real-world applications by providing accurate location estimates for a mobile robot in various navigation scenarios. The source code for EMA-VIO is made available online. 

In addition to EMA-VIO, another approach called Memory-augmented Visual-inertial Odometry (MVO) is also introduced in the study. Although MVO delivers superior performance, its complexity limits its application to mobile agents. Contrarily, the simpler MVO variant, EMA-VIO, experiences difficulties in model training due to its extensive number of parameters. To overcome these training challenges, the study presents an optimized version of MVO called Optimized Memory-augmented Visual-inertial Odometry (OMVO), which achieves a balance between performance and complexity by simplifying the data batch size and introducing a linear interpolation technique. The study evaluates both the original MVO and the OMVO variant, with the latter demonstrating its effectiveness in real-world applications. The source code for both MVO and OMVO is made available online.

We've developed a novel theoretical framework that extends the Weyl's anomaly to a higher order, achieving this through the application of the Reimann-Liouville derivative. This framework is relevant to three- and higher-dimensional materials and is represented by an exact Lagrangian density in 't Hooft's gauge. We derive the charge conjugation and parity operators, as well as the conserved higher-order current, which is conserved in the presence of a gradient of chemical potentials. We also develop a linear response theory to describe the transport properties of these materials, and we show that the coefficient of the linear response is an exact integral of a new quadratic density over energy, which is a result that is unaffected by the Reimann-Liouville derivative. We analyze a specific model of three-dimensional square-root higher-order Weyl materials and calculate its energy density and pressure, as well as the anomalous velocity. We find that the Reimann-Liouville derivative can be interpreted as a non-local chemical potential that arises from the interaction of the Weyl fermions with a bosonic field. We also demonstrate that the Reimann-Liouville derivative can be related to a non-trivial topological invariant, which results in the restoration of the fermi surface and the generation of a non-trivial density of states. This leads to the enhancement of the anomalous velocity over a critical density of non-zero energy, and it suggests that the materials possess a unique square-root higher-order non-Abelian Hall effect. The theoretical framework can be applied to describe the behavior of square-root higher-order Weyl materials in both their zero-doped and doping states. The materials exhibit a critical density below which the anomalous velocity is increased by an amount that is proportional to the square of the density of non-zero energy, and in this regime, the Reimann-Liouville derivative dominates the transport properties. Above the critical density, the anomalous velocity returns to its initial proportional relationship with the square of the density of non-zero energy, and it becomes insensitive to the Reimann-Liouville derivative. The description of the materials' behavior relies on a unique interplay between their non-Abelian Hall effect and the Reimann-Liouville derivative, and it results from the application of the Reimann-Liouville derivative to the higher-order Weyl's anomaly. The materials' behavior can be manipulated by adjusting the density of non-zero energy, which allows for the transition between two distinct regimes of transport properties.
